tales.title: The Women of the Palace Drill
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
King Helü of Wu had read the thirteen chapters of a wandering strategist named Sun Wu, and he was curious, perhaps a little mischievous. "Your book is fine," he said. "But could you show me its method on something small? On the women of my palace, say?"

Sun Wu bowed. "I could."

So one hundred and eighty palace ladies were led out into the courtyard in silks and hairpins, and each was handed a halberd. Sun Wu divided them into two companies and made the king's two favourite concubines their captains. Then, slowly and plainly, he explained the drill. "Do you know where your heart is, and your left hand, your right hand, your back?" They did. "When the drum sounds for front, face your heart. For left, face your left hand. For right, your right. For rear, turn to your back." He repeated the instructions three times, and set the executioner's axes beside the drum.

The drum sounded: "Right!" The courtyard dissolved into laughter.

"If the orders are not clear and the commands not understood," said Sun Wu, "the fault is the general's." He explained everything again, five times over. The drum sounded: "Left!" And again the ladies collapsed in giggles, the two captains loudest of all.

"Now the orders are clear," said Sun Wu, "and still they are not carried out. The fault is the officers'." He ordered the two captains beheaded.

From his pavilion the king saw what was happening and sent a messenger running. "We already know the general can command! Without these two women, food will have no taste for us. Spare them."

"Your servant has received his commission as general," Sun Wu replied, "and a general in the field does not take every order from his lord." The two favourites died. He appointed the next two in line as captains and sounded the drum once more.

Left, right, front, rear, kneel, rise: the women moved as one body, without a sound, without a single error. Sun Wu reported to the king that the troops were ready; they would go through fire and water at his word.

The king, sulking, said he had no wish to come down and look. "Your Majesty loves words," said Sun Wu, "but cannot put them to use." Yet Helü knew what he had seen, and he made Sun Wu his general. Within a few years the armies of Wu had broken mighty Chu and marched into its capital.
tales.lesson: Rules only bind when they are first made perfectly clear and then truly enforced; a leader must own unclear orders but cannot excuse ignored ones.
tales.why: Sunzi's reckoning asks "Whose laws and orders are carried out?" and counts "strictness" among the commander's virtues; the drill shows both, along with the good faith of explaining the orders before enforcing them.
tales.living: Where in your work or home do you announce expectations but never quite hold anyone, including yourself, to them?

tales.title: Three Horses, Three Races
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
In the state of Qi, the great lords had a passion for horse racing, and General Tian Ji had a passion for losing to them. Again and again he matched his teams against those of King Wei and the princes, wagering heavy sums of gold, and again and again he went home poorer.

The races were run in three heats. Each side fielded a top team, a middle team and a bottom team of chariot horses, and the custom was to run them like against like: best against best, middling against middling, worst against worst. The king's stables were richer than Tian Ji's, so in every pairing the king's horses were a little faster. Not by much. By enough.

At that time Tian Ji was sheltering a guest, a man named Sun Bin, who had come to Qi hidden in an envoy's carriage. His feet had been cut away by a jealous rival in the state of Wei, and he could no longer walk unaided; but there was nothing wrong with his eyes. He went to the races and watched carefully, and he noticed what Tian Ji had never bothered to notice: the gap between the two stables was small, and it was the same in every class.

"Next time," Sun Bin told him, "bet everything you have. I can make you win."

Tian Ji trusted him and laid down a thousand pieces of gold. The king, amused, accepted.

"Now," said Sun Bin quietly before the first heat, "take your worst team and set it against the king's best."

The crowd thought the general had lost his wits. His slow horses trailed home far behind the king's champions, and the courtiers laughed. Then Tian Ji sent his best team against the king's middle team, and won. Then he sent his middle team against the king's worst, and won again.

Two races to one. The same horses, the same track, the same king. Tian Ji collected his thousand pieces of gold.

King Wei was not angry; he was intrigued. He asked who had devised such a thing, and Tian Ji brought the crippled guest before him. The king questioned Sun Bin about the arts of war, listened long, and made him his teacher. Years later, carried to battle in a covered cart, Sun Bin would plan the campaigns that broke the armies of Wei, the very state that had maimed him.
tales.lesson: Before any contest, lay the two sides out honestly, piece by piece; a careful count often reveals a winning arrangement that raw strength would never find.
tales.why: Sun Bin did what verse 1.7 asks, comparing the sides by reckoning to "search out how things truly stand", and so put more "counting rods on his side" before a single horse ran (1.12).
tales.living: In a contest you keep losing, have you ever listed your strengths and theirs side by side and asked whether you are simply matching them in the wrong order?

tales.title: The Gift on the Empty Shore
tales.source: Virgil, Aeneid; Homer, Odyssey (legend)
tales.tale:
For ten years the Greeks had camped on the beach before Troy, and for ten years the walls had held. Heroes had died on both sides. Achilles was dead, and Hector. The siege had become a habit, like weather.

Then one morning the Trojan lookouts rubbed their eyes. The Greek camp was ash. The black ships were gone from the shore. The plain, trampled for a decade, lay silent under the gulls. And in the middle of it, where the tents had stood, rose an enormous horse built of fir planks, taller than a house, its head turned towards the city.

The gates opened for the first time in years. Trojans poured out, laughing, walking where the enemy had walked, pointing out where Achilles had pitched his tent. They circled the horse. Some wanted to burn it, some to hurl it from a cliff, some to drag it into the city as a trophy. The priest Laocoön ran down from the citadel shouting that this was a trick, that he feared the Greeks even bearing gifts, and he flung a spear into the horse's flank. It quivered there, and the hollow wood boomed.

Just then shepherds dragged forward a ragged prisoner, a Greek named Sinon, who wept and told a careful story. His countrymen had sailed home in despair, he said. They had meant to sacrifice him for a fair wind and he had escaped. The horse was an offering to the goddess Athena, built huge on purpose so that the Trojans could never fit it through their gates; for if it ever stood inside Troy, the city could never fall.

Then two serpents rose out of the sea and killed Laocoön and his sons. The Trojans, terrified, took it for a sign. They broke open a section of their own wall and hauled the horse inside on rollers, with garlands and singing. Four times it stuck at the threshold, and four times something clashed within; nobody listened.

That night the city feasted and slept, drunk on peace. Sinon crept to the horse and slid back a hidden bolt. Out of its belly, down a rope, came Odysseus and his chosen men. They killed the sleepy guards and threw open the gates, and the Greek fleet, which had been waiting all along behind the nearby island of Tenedos, rowed back in the dark.

By dawn Troy was burning.
tales.lesson: An opponent who believes you have gone is an opponent who has stopped watching; appearing weak, absent or finished can open doors that strength never could.
tales.why: The Greeks lived out "near, seem far" (1.9), vanishing from the shore while hiding off Tenedos, and then struck "where they are unready" (1.11), on the one night Troy thought the war was over.
tales.living: When something you were braced against suddenly seems to vanish, do you relax at once, or do you ask what changed and why?

tales.title: The King Who Tested the Oracle
tales.source: Herodotus, Histories, Book I
tales.tale:
Croesus of Lydia was the richest man alive, and he was not a fool. When the Persians under Cyrus began to swell beyond the river Halys, he wanted advice, and he wanted to be sure the advice was good. So he devised a test. He sent envoys to seven oracles with orders to count the days, and on the hundredth day to ask: what is the king of Lydia doing at this moment?

On that day Croesus did the strangest thing he could think of. He chopped up a tortoise and a lamb and boiled them together in a bronze cauldron with a bronze lid. Only the priestess at Delphi answered rightly: she smelt the tortoise in its shell, she said, seething with the flesh of a lamb, bronze below and bronze above.

Delighted, Croesus poured gold into Delphi and asked his true question. Should he march against Persia? The answer came back: if Croesus crosses the Halys, he will destroy a great empire. He asked again, how long his own rule would last. Until a mule sits on the throne of the Medes, said the priestess. A mule as king! Croesus laughed and called up his army.

He crossed the river and met Cyrus at Pteria. The day ended with neither side broken. Croesus, finding his army smaller than he liked, marched home to Sardis, sent his hired soldiers away for the winter and wrote to his allies to gather in the spring. Wars, he reckoned, waited for good weather.

Cyrus did not wait. He followed straight on Croesus's heels and appeared before Sardis while the allies were still reading their letters. On the plain outside the city he set his baggage camels in front of his line, and the Lydian horses, which had never smelt a camel, wheeled and bolted. Within two weeks the citadel had fallen.

The oracle had been right after all. A great empire was destroyed: his own. And Cyrus, born of a Median mother and a Persian father, was the mule. Croesus had checked the soothsayer with great cunning. He had never once checked the man he was about to fight.
tales.lesson: Careful reckoning means weighing the real enemy, the real ground and your own real strength, not seeking a promise that you will win.
tales.why: Croesus counted everything except what Sunzi says to count: he never asked "Whose forces are stronger?" or how Cyrus would move, and so he went to war with no true count at all, and Sunzi asks "how much worse to have no count at all!"
tales.living: Where are you looking for reassurance about a decision when you should be looking hard at the facts?

tales.title: The River on Christmas Night
tales.source: American Revolutionary War (Battle of Trenton, 1776)
tales.tale:
By December 1776 the American army looked finished. It had been beaten out of New York and chased across New Jersey; its men were ragged, some marching barefoot on frozen ground, and most of their enlistments ran out on the last day of the year. Across the Delaware River, the British settled into winter quarters, certain the rebellion would melt with the snow. At Trenton they left a garrison of Hessian soldiers under Colonel Johann Rall, a brave officer who thought so little of the Americans that he never troubled to build earthworks.

George Washington knew what everyone thought of his army, and he decided to use it. Who keeps watch against a corpse?

On Christmas night he gathered some two and a half thousand men at McConkey's Ferry. The plan was to cross by midnight and strike at dawn. Then the weather turned: wind, sleet and snow drove across the water, and slabs of ice ground against the heavy black boats. Fishermen from Massachusetts poled and rowed through the dark, horses and cannon lurching aboard, hour after hour. The crossing ran three hours late. Two other columns meant to join the attack could not get over at all.

A cautious man would have turned back. Washington marched on through nine miles of storm, the password passing from mouth to mouth: Victory or Death. Men's feet left blood on the road.

The same storm that cost him his timetable also blinded the Hessians. Who would attack in such weather? Their patrols had come in; their sentries huddled. Shortly after eight in the morning the Americans came down the two roads into Trenton at once, and cannon swept the main streets before the Hessians could form. Rall tried to rally his men in an orchard and fell, mortally wounded. Within about an hour it was over. Close to nine hundred Hessians were taken prisoner. The Americans lost hardly a man in the fight.

The news ran through the colonies like a spark. Men whose time was up agreed to stay, and the army that everyone had buried was alive again.
tales.lesson: An opponent who has written you off stops guarding against you; the moment you seem weakest can be the moment to strike where no one is looking.
tales.why: Washington's army, "able, seem unable", let the Hessians relax; then he struck through a storm, "where they are unready" and when they did not look.
tales.living: Where might others' low expectations of you be the very opening you need?

tales.title: Another Such Victory
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus
tales.tale:
Pyrrhus, King of Epirus, was thought by many in his day to be the finest general alive. Hannibal himself, it was said, later ranked him among the very greatest. So when the Greek city of Tarentum in southern Italy begged him to come and save it from the Romans, he came, with some twenty-five thousand men and a herd of war elephants that no Roman soldier had ever seen.

At Heraclea, in 280 BC, he met the legions by a river. The fight swayed back and forth for hours, and Pyrrhus had his horse killed under him; but in the end he loosed his elephants, and the Roman cavalry, whose horses bolted at the smell and sight of the beasts, broke. The field was his.

Yet when he walked among the dead he was thoughtful. The Romans had fallen where they stood, every wound in front. And his own losses were heavy, many of them the veteran officers and friends he had brought from home, men he could not replace across the sea.

Rome did not sue for peace. Rome raised new legions.

The next year, at Asculum, it happened again. Two days of grinding battle; elephants; a Roman retreat; a victory for Pyrrhus. His men crowded around to congratulate him, and Plutarch tells us that the king answered: "If we are victorious in one more battle with the Romans, we shall be utterly ruined."

For Rome seemed to have soldiers as a fountain has water. Every defeat they suffered was refilled from the farms of Latium; every loss Pyrrhus suffered was a hole in his army that stayed open. His Italian allies grew sullen at the cost. Restless, he crossed to Sicily to fight Carthage instead, won more battles, quarrelled with the Sicilian Greeks, and came back to Italy with a smaller, wearier army than before.

At Beneventum in 275 BC the Romans, now less frightened of elephants, finally held him. Pyrrhus sailed home to Greece, having spent six years, a fortune and the best of his men in Italy, and owning almost nothing there to show for it. He died a few years later in a street fight in Argos, struck by a roof tile thrown by an old woman.

Two thousand years on, his name still lives in English, attached to a single phrase: a Pyrrhic victory.
tales.lesson: A campaign can win every battle and still lose the war if each win costs more than you can replace; count the cost, not just the score.
tales.why: Pyrrhus won, yet saw "weapons dull, edges blunt" and "strength drained" (2.2), the proof that "no state has ever profited from a long war" (2.3).
tales.living: Which of your recent wins, at work or in an argument, cost you more in energy, goodwill or money than it was really worth?

tales.title: The Road to Handan
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian); Strategies of the Warring States
tales.tale:
In 260 BC the armies of Qin and Zhao faced each other at Changping, and for nearly three years neither moved. The old Zhao general Lian Po sat behind his ramparts and refused battle, while Qin hauled grain over the mountains and Zhao hauled grain over the plains, and both states bled their farmers dry to feed the soldiers.

Then Zhao lost patience. Its king replaced cautious Lian Po with young Zhao Kuo, who had read every book on war and fought no battles. The Qin general Bai Qi lured him out, cut his supply lines and starved his army in the valleys. The young man died at the head of a final charge; the rest surrendered. It was the bloodiest victory of the age.

The Qin court was jubilant. Surely Zhao's capital, Handan, now lay open. The next year Qin's armies marched on it.

But Bai Qi, the victor himself, refused to lead them. He was summoned and pleaded illness. The king's minister came to his house in person, and the general explained himself plainly. "At Changping we won, but more than half our own men are dead. The state is empty. The people are worn out. Now we would cross mountains and rivers to besiege another kingdom's capital. Zhao will fight from inside its walls and the lords outside will come to help it. I see no victory there."

Qin went anyway. Handan's people, with nothing left to lose, tore down their own houses for timber to stoke the defences and ate what could not be eaten. Months became a year, then two. Qin's grain carts crawled over the mountains. Its soldiers sickened.

And the neighbours came, just as Bai Qi had said. In Wei, a prince named Lord Xinling stole his own king's tally of command, took over an army that had been ordered to stand still, and marched it to Handan. Chu sent troops too. In 257 BC the relief forces fell upon the exhausted besiegers and broke them. Qin's army streamed home in disorder.

The king of Qin, furious and ashamed, turned on the general who had warned him. Bai Qi was stripped of rank, sent into exile and, on the road out of the capital, handed a sword with which to end his own life.

Qin would one day unify all China. But it would wait another generation to do it.
tales.lesson: A great victory followed by a long, draining campaign can hand the prize to the neighbours who stood aside; knowing when your strength is spent is part of winning.
tales.why: Qin's siege of Handan shows exactly how "neighbouring lords rise to profit from your exhaustion" (2.2), and why Sunzi says to "prize victory, not duration" (2.9).
tales.living: After your last big push at work or at home, did you rest and rebuild, or did you charge straight into the next fight on an empty tank?

tales.title: The Emperor Who Counted the Dead
tales.source: Edicts of Ashoka (Rock Edict XIII)
tales.tale:
Eight years after he was crowned, the emperor Ashoka of the Mauryas turned his armies on Kalinga, the proud coastal kingdom on India's eastern shore that had never bowed to his family. His grandfather had built the empire with the sword; his father had widened it. Kalinga was the piece that did not fit, and Ashoka meant to make it fit.

He did. The war was won, and Kalinga became a province. By every measure kings had always used, it was a triumph.

But Ashoka did a thing kings seldom do: he counted. Not the treasure, not the new taxes, but the people. And years later he had the numbers carved in stone so that no one could forget them. A hundred and fifty thousand people, his edict says, were carried away from Kalinga as captives. A hundred thousand were killed. Many times that number died afterwards, of hunger and sickness and the long ruin that follows an army.

He did not stop there. He thought of the good people of Kalinga, the priests and ascetics, the households that honoured their parents and treated servants kindly, who had done nothing at all, and who now mourned a husband, a son, a friend. Even those who had escaped unharmed, he wrote, suffered when misfortune fell on those they loved. All of this, the stone says, weighed heavily on the mind of the Beloved of the Gods.

So the conqueror laid down conquest. He declared that from now on the only victory worth having was the victory of dhamma, of right conduct. He sent out officers not to collect tribute but to look after the welfare of the people. He had wells dug and shade trees planted along the roads, rest houses built, medicine provided for people and for animals. He sent envoys to kings far to the west, carrying not threats but teaching.

The rock edicts still stand, scattered across the subcontinent, weathered and cracked. Most monuments to victory boast of how many were slain. Ashoka's is the rare one that grieves.
tales.lesson: The true cost of a fight is paid long after it is won, and mostly by people who never chose it; only by counting that cost can you know whether a fight is worth having.
tales.why: Ashoka grasped what Sunzi warns of, the fields where "seven parts in ten are gone", and having fully grasped "the harm of arms" he understood their use well enough to set them aside.
tales.living: When you last won an argument or a battle at work, who paid for it that you did not count?

tales.title: The Archer Who Shot the Khan's Horse
tales.source: The Secret History of the Mongols
tales.tale:
Around the year 1201, on the steppe of Mongolia, the young chief Temüjin fought the Tayichiud clan, the kinsmen who had once hunted him as a boy. In the thick of the battle an arrow came out of the enemy ranks and struck Temüjin's war horse, a fine fallow mount with a white muzzle, in the neck. The horse went down. Temüjin survived, and the Tayichiud were broken and scattered.

Afterwards the defeated men came in to surrender, and Temüjin asked them a question. Who, he said, shot my horse from the top of the ridge?

It would have been easy to keep quiet. The archer was surely dead, or fled, or lost in the crowd of captives. Instead a man stepped forward. His name was Jirqo'adai, of the Besüt people. It was I who shot, he said. If the Khan wishes to kill me, my blood will soak a patch of earth the size of a palm. If he spares me, I will ride before him; I will cut through deep water for him and smash bright rock to pieces.

The men around Temüjin waited for the order. An enemy who had nearly killed their chief now stood unarmed before him, admitting it to his face.

Temüjin looked at him for a long moment. A man who fights his enemy, he said, usually hides what he has done and keeps his mouth shut for fear. This one does not hide; he tells me plainly. He is a man worth having as a companion. And then he gave him a new name: Jebe, which means the arrowhead, in memory of the arrow he had loosed.

Jebe kept his word. He became one of the great generals of the Mongol empire, one of the four the Secret History calls Temüjin's hounds. He chased down rival khans across the mountains of Central Asia, and with Sübe'etei he led the famous ride round the Caspian Sea, thousands of miles through lands no Mongol army had seen.

The arrow that nearly ended Temüjin's story became one of the sharpest in his quiver.
tales.lesson: Defeat an opponent and then treat them well, and you may gain a strength you could never have hired; the enemy you win over can serve you better than one you destroy.
tales.why: Sunzi advises to "treat the captured soldiers well and keep them", calling it "defeating the enemy and growing stronger", and Temüjin did exactly that with the very man who had shot at him.
tales.living: Is there a former rival, critic or competitor whose talent you could win to your side instead of keeping at a distance?

tales.title: The Long Road to Ming
tales.source: Japanese and Korean history (Imjin War, 1592 to 1598)
tales.tale:
In 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a foot soldier's son who had risen to rule all Japan, found himself with a unified country and a vast army with nothing left to fight. His ambition looked further: across the sea to Korea, and beyond Korea to the throne of Ming China itself.

In the spring of 1592 his armies landed at Busan, well over a hundred thousand men, hardened by a century of civil war and armed with muskets. At first everything went brilliantly. Seoul fell in about three weeks; Pyongyang soon after. The generals sent home glowing reports.

But every bowl of rice, every barrel of powder, every replacement horse had to come across the strait and then be carried up hundreds of miles of mountain roads. And at sea there was Admiral Yi Sun-sin. With his armoured turtle ships and a fleet that knew every island and tide of the southern coast, Yi fell on the Japanese transports again and again, and the supplies meant to sail up the west coast never came. Ashore, Korean irregulars burned granaries and ambushed columns. Then a great Ming army crossed the Yalu.

Winter in the north froze men in their quilted armour. The army that had raced to Pyongyang fell back towards the coast, and the war sank into years of truce talks, sieges and envoys. In 1597 Hideyoshi sent his armies back for a second invasion. It ground on, bloody and fruitless, until he died in the autumn of 1598, and his council quietly brought the soldiers home.

Six years of fighting had gained Japan nothing. The great lords of the west, Hideyoshi's surest supporters, had spent their men and their fortunes overseas. One great lord had sent no troops across the sea at all: Tokugawa Ieyasu, who had waited at home with his strength intact.

Two years after Hideyoshi's death, at Sekigahara, Ieyasu defeated the coalition loyal to Hideyoshi's young son. His family would rule Japan for more than two and a half centuries. The heirs of the man who meant to conquer China were swept away by the one rival who had stayed at home.
tales.lesson: A long, distant campaign drains you faster than it drains your enemy, and the one who profits is often a rival who simply stayed out and kept their strength.
tales.why: Hideyoshi's armies were bled by "distant haulage", and when strength was drained and treasure gone, a neighbouring lord, Ieyasu, did indeed "rise to profit from your exhaustion".
tales.living: Which drawn-out project or quarrel is quietly spending resources that someone else will one day profit from?

tales.title: The War Fought on a Tabletop
tales.source: Mozi, chapter 'Gongshu'
tales.tale:
The master craftsman Gongshu Ban, whose carpentry was legend, had built a marvel for the King of Chu: the cloud ladder, a great wheeled siege tower that could carry men up and over any wall. Chu meant to use it against the small state of Song.

The philosopher Mozi heard of this in his own country far to the north. He set out at once and walked for ten days and ten nights without resting, tearing strips from his robe to bind his bleeding feet, until he reached the Chu capital and Gongshu Ban's door.

"There is a man in the north who has insulted me," he said. "I would like you to kill him for me."

Gongshu Ban was offended. "My principles forbid me to kill a man."

Mozi bowed twice. "Then let me ask about your principles. Song has done nothing to Chu. Chu has more land than it can farm and fewer people than it needs; to spend what it lacks fighting for what it already has too much of is not wise. To attack a blameless state is not humane. You will not kill one man, yet you will help kill many. Is that principle?"

Gongshu Ban had no answer, but said the king had decided. So Mozi went to the king, who listened, agreed with every word, and still said: "Gongshu Ban has made me cloud ladders. I shall take Song."

Mozi untied his belt and laid it in a loop on the floor. "This is the wall of Song," he said. He took a handful of wooden writing slips. "These are my engines of defence. Let Master Gongshu attack."

There, before the king, the craftsman set out his ladders and rams nine times, by nine different methods. Nine times Mozi turned him back. When Gongshu Ban's devices were exhausted, Mozi still had defences in hand.

Gongshu Ban said slowly, "I know a way to beat you. I won't say what it is."

"I know your way too," said Mozi. "You mean to kill me. But my disciple Qin Guli and three hundred of my students are already standing on the walls of Song with my engines, waiting for Chu. Kill me, and you will still not win."

The king of Chu said, "Very well. I will not attack Song."

On his way home Mozi passed through Song in a downpour and asked to shelter in a gateway. The gatekeeper, who had no idea what had happened, turned him away.
tales.lesson: The cheapest war is the one stopped while it is still a plan; show an opponent, convincingly, that their scheme cannot work and they may abandon it of their own accord.
tales.why: Mozi struck at Chu's plan and at its confidence, never at an army, which is what verse 3.3 calls the highest warfare that "strikes at plans"; he bent the enemy "without a battle" (3.2).
tales.living: Is there a conflict brewing around you that a calm demonstration, made now and in private, could end before anyone takes sides?

tales.title: A Letter Instead of an Army
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
In 204 BC the general Han Xin, fighting for the future founder of the Han dynasty, had just won one of the most famous battles in Chinese history. At Jingxing Pass he had set his outnumbered army with its back to a river, so that no man could flee, and while they fought for their lives his hidden cavalry slipped into the enemy's empty camp and raised two thousand red banners there. The army of Zhao, seeing its own camp taken, broke apart.

Among the prisoners was Li Zuoche, Lord of Guangwu, the one adviser in the Zhao camp whose plan, had it been heeded, might have destroyed Han Xin. Han Xin had offered a thousand pieces of gold for him alive. When Li Zuoche was dragged in, bound, the general untied him with his own hands, seated him facing east in the place of a teacher and asked: "I want to march north against Yan and east against Qi. How should I do it?"

At first Li Zuoche refused. "A defeated general," he said, "has no right to speak of courage." Han Xin pressed him, and at last he spoke.

"Your name now shakes the world. But your men are exhausted. If you lead tired troops against the strong walls of Yan, you may fail to take them, and the moment Yan sees you cannot, it will grow bold, and Qi will stiffen behind it. Then your weakness will be on show for all.

"Instead, rest your soldiers. Calm Zhao. Feast the troops and look after the orphans of the dead. Then point your army north as if you were coming, and send a single envoy with a letter to Yan, setting out your strengths. Yan will not dare to refuse. Armies, they say, may first make a show and only afterwards fight."

Han Xin answered, "Good," and did exactly as he was told. His soldiers ate and slept, his banners faced north, and a messenger rode to the court of Yan with a letter.

Yan read it, weighed the general who had just shattered Zhao, and submitted, as the record says, the way grass bends before the wind. Not a city was stormed. Not a soldier was lost. The whole state passed into Han's hands whole, its fields, its granaries and its fighting men intact.
tales.lesson: Winning whole is better than winning by ruin; a reputation, a pause and a well-made offer can bring in what a battle would only break.
tales.why: Yan was taken "intact" rather than shattered (3.1), a state brought down "without long campaigns" so that "the gain is complete" (3.5).
tales.living: Is there something you are about to force, a negotiation, a decision, a change at home, that a patient, well-framed request might win without any damage at all?

tales.title: The Wind, the Sun and the Traveller's Cloak
tales.source: Aesop
tales.tale:
High above a winding road, the North Wind and the Sun fell into an argument about which of them was the stronger. The Wind blustered that it could snap oaks and sink fleets. The Sun only smiled and said that strength was easier to claim than to prove.

Just then a traveller came along the road below, a man in a thick woollen cloak, trudging towards the next village.

"There," said the Sun. "Whichever of us can take that cloak off his back is the stronger. You may go first."

The Wind drew itself up. It came down the hillside in a cold gust that lifted the dust and set the hedges hissing. The traveller shivered and pulled his cloak a little tighter. The Wind blew harder. Branches bent, dry leaves whirled up in spirals, the man's hat went tumbling away across a field. He let it go, put his head down and clutched his cloak with both fists.

The Wind roared. It howled through the valley until the birds took shelter and the sheep huddled behind the walls, and it tore at the traveller's cloak from every side, from below, from above, in sudden twisting blasts. The harder it pulled, the harder he held. In the end he wrapped the cloak twice around himself, knotted the corners and crouched against a stone wall, and the Wind, out of breath, had to give up.

"Your turn," it gasped.

The Sun came out from behind a cloud and simply shone. Nothing more. The air on the road grew mild. The traveller straightened, loosened the knot, let the cloak hang open. The Sun shone a little warmer. The man wiped his forehead, slowed his pace, unfastened the clasp and slung the cloak over one arm. Before long the road was so hot that he looked about him, spotted a stream shaded by willows, threw the cloak on the grass, and waded in up to his knees with a sigh of pure relief.

The Sun said nothing at all. It did not need to.
tales.lesson: Force provokes resistance; changing the conditions so the other side wants to yield gets you what you want with nothing broken.
tales.why: The Sun wins the contest with no struggle, the "summit of skill" of bending the opponent "without a battle" (3.2), and nothing is worn down so "the gain is complete" (3.5).
tales.living: With someone you are trying to persuade right now, are you blowing harder, or could you change the climate so they choose to let go?

tales.title: The Hare Who Spoke for the Moon
tales.source: Indian folk tale (Panchatantra)
tales.tale:
Once a great drought fell upon the forest. Ponds shrank to cracked mud and the streams fell silent, and the elephants, led by their huge old king, wandered thirsty for days. At last a scout came back with good news: beyond the hills lay a lake that never dried, deep and cool, so lovely that it was called the Lake of the Moon.

The herd set off at once. But all around that lake lived a nation of hares, and their burrows lay in the soft earth by the water. The elephants came crashing down to drink, and they did not look where they put their feet. Hares were crushed in their homes; others limped away with broken legs.

That night the surviving hares met in council. Some wanted to flee; some wept. What could a hare do against an elephant? Then a clever old hare called Vijaya spoke. Leave it to me, he said. I will go as an envoy.

He did not walk up to the elephant king, who might have trodden on him without noticing. He climbed a high rock beside the path and called down in a grave voice. O king of elephants, I am the messenger of the Moon himself. He who lives in this lake is angry. You have trampled his hares, and the hare is the Moon's own creature: look, he carries one in his face. He commands you to leave his lake, or suffer.

The elephant was shaken. Where is your lord? he asked. Show me, and I will beg his pardon.

Vijaya led him alone to the water's edge in the night. There in the still lake shone the full moon. The elephant bowed to the reflection and stretched out his trunk to touch the water in reverence. The surface shivered and the moon broke into a hundred trembling pieces.

See, said the hare quietly, how angry he is that you have touched his water.

The elephant king backed away in terror, bowed again and again, and led his whole herd out of that country, never to return. And the hares lived on in peace by the Lake of the Moon.
tales.lesson: Strength need not meet strength; the weakest party can win by changing what the stronger one believes, without a single blow.
tales.why: The hares could never fight the elephants, so Vijaya struck "at plans": he changed the king's mind about where he was and whom he had offended, and bent the herd "without a battle".
tales.living: In a contest you cannot win by force, what belief on the other side could you change instead?

tales.title: A Telegram from Rome
tales.source: First Italo-Ethiopian War (Battle of Adwa, 1896)
tales.tale:
In February 1896 General Oreste Baratieri sat in his camp in the northern highlands of Ethiopia with about seventeen thousand Italian and Eritrean soldiers. A few miles off, around the town of Adwa, lay the army of the Emperor Menelik II: perhaps a hundred thousand men, many armed with modern rifles that Menelik had patiently bought from Europe over many years.

Baratieri did not want to attack. He was short of food, but so was Menelik, and an army that size could not stay in one place for long. If both sides simply waited, the Ethiopian host might have to break up and go home to feed itself. Baratieri was weighing a retreat to better ground.

In Rome, Prime Minister Francesco Crispi had no patience for weighing. He had promised Italians an empire and needed a victory. In the last days of February a telegram reached the camp, scorching the general for what Crispi called a military consumption, a wasting disease, and demanding some plan of action. Unknown to Baratieri's men, the government had already dispatched another general to replace him.

Baratieri called his brigade commanders together. They were eager for glory and voted to advance. On the night of 29 February the Italians marched out in three columns over unknown mountain country, guided by poor maps. In the darkness the brigade of General Albertone took a wrong valley and pressed on far ahead of the rest, alone.

At dawn on 1 March, Menelik's army, warned by its scouts and waiting in the hills, fell on Albertone's isolated brigade and broke it. Then it turned on the other columns one by one, before they could support each other. Empress Taytu herself had come with her own troops; Ethiopian horsemen swept the flanks. By afternoon the Italian army had ceased to exist. Thousands lay dead on the slopes; the survivors streamed back towards Eritrea.

When the news reached Rome, crowds filled the streets and Crispi fell from power within days. That autumn Italy signed a treaty recognising Ethiopia's full independence. Adwa became a beacon for people across Africa: the day a European army was beaten in open battle.
tales.lesson: Decisions about a fight belong to those who can see the ground; when a distant boss overrides a commander's judgment to satisfy his own impatience, the battle is half lost before it begins.
tales.why: Crispi, "not knowing the army cannot advance", ordered it forward and left its commander in doubt; Menelik, meanwhile, "waits, prepared, for the unprepared".
tales.living: Are you pushing someone closer to the work to act on your timetable rather than theirs, or being pushed that way yourself?

tales.title: The General Who Would Not Fight
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
Li Mu commanded Zhao's northern frontier at Yanmen, where the grasslands met the farms and the Xiongnu horsemen rode in each year to raid.

He ran his command as a household. The market taxes of the frontier went straight into his own headquarters, and every day oxen were slaughtered to feed the soldiers. He drilled them in archery and riding, built beacon towers across the hills and kept spies far out on the plain. And he gave one strict order: "When the Xiongnu raid, pull everyone and everything inside the walls at once. Any man who dares to go out and take a prisoner will be beheaded."

So for years, whenever the beacons flared, the herds were driven in, the gates were shut, and the raiders found nothing to take. Zhao lost almost nothing. But the Xiongnu laughed at Li Mu for a coward, and so, in time, did his own soldiers. The King of Zhao sent him angry rebukes. Li Mu went on as before. At last the king recalled him and sent a bolder man.

The new general rode out every time the Xiongnu came. He fought often and lost often. Men died; cattle were carried off; the frontier farmers could no longer plant. Within a year the king was begging Li Mu to return. Li Mu shut his door and claimed illness. When he was finally forced to go, he set one condition: "If I am to command, I must do as I did before." The king agreed.

Back at Yanmen, he did as he had done. The Xiongnu came, took nothing and went away, still laughing. Meanwhile his soldiers, fed and paid and rewarded for years without ever being allowed to fight, began to ache for battle.

Then Li Mu chose them: thirteen hundred chariots, thirteen thousand horsemen, fifty thousand picked men who had won rewards, a hundred thousand archers. He turned the herds out to graze until the plain was covered with cattle and people. When a small band of Xiongnu rode in, he sent a few thousand men to meet them, lose, and flee, leaving the herds behind.

The Chanyu heard, and came down with his whole host. Li Mu was waiting. He spread out his wings, closed them from left and right, and destroyed more than a hundred thousand of the Xiongnu horsemen.

For more than ten years afterwards they did not dare come near Zhao's border.
tales.lesson: First make yourself impossible to beat, and then be patient; the opponent's overconfidence will give you the opening that no amount of eager fighting could.
tales.why: Li Mu did as the masters of old, who "first made themselves unbeatable, then waited for the enemy to become beatable" (4.1); his army "wins first, then seeks battle" (4.5), while his impatient replacement fought first and looked for a way to win.
tales.living: Where are you being pressured to act before your foundations are ready, and what would it take to hold steady a little longer?

tales.title: Hannibal's Shadow
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Fabius; Livy
tales.tale:
In 217 BC Rome was in shock. Hannibal had crossed the Alps with his elephants, smashed one Roman army at the Trebia and then trapped another in the morning fog beside Lake Trasimene, where it was cut to pieces. The road to Rome lay open. The Senate named a dictator: Quintus Fabius Maximus, a slow-spoken, careful man whose childhood nickname had been Little Lamb.

Fabius did something no Roman general had ever done. He marched out with his army and refused to fight.

He followed Hannibal everywhere, always on the high ground, always close enough to watch and never close enough to be caught. When Carthaginian foragers wandered, his cavalry snapped them up. When Hannibal offered battle on the open plain where his African horsemen ruled, Fabius stayed in the hills. When Hannibal burned the rich farms of Fabius's friends to provoke him, and pointedly left his own estates untouched to make Rome suspect him, Fabius sold the estates to ransom Roman prisoners and kept on waiting.

Rome hated it. The soldiers called him Hannibal's tutor, the slave who walks behind a boy carrying his books. In the city they said he was a coward, or a traitor. The Senate split his command and gave half to his brash master of horse, Minucius, who promptly marched out to fight and was lured into a trap, his men encircled on a hillside. Fabius came down from the heights, drove Hannibal off and saved them. Minucius led his soldiers to Fabius's camp and greeted him as father.

But the dictatorship ran out. The next year the people elected consuls who promised to finish Hannibal in a single blow. At Cannae, in 216 BC, they led the largest army Rome had ever raised against him, and in one summer afternoon he surrounded it and destroyed it. Tens of thousands died.

After Cannae, Rome went back to Fabius's way. No more great pitched battles against Hannibal in Italy; only shadowing, harassing, wearing down. Hannibal stayed in Italy for another dozen years, winning skirmishes and holding ground, and yet he never took Rome, and in the end he sailed home to Africa to defend Carthage.

The poet Ennius wrote one line for Fabius that Romans quoted for centuries: one man, by delaying, restored the state.
tales.lesson: When you are the weaker side, survive first; keeping yourself whole is what lets the stronger side's advantages run out.
tales.why: Fabius made Rome "unbeatable" by refusing the battles it could only lose, defending because "strength falls short" (4.2), and waited for Hannibal to become "beatable" (4.1).
tales.living: When the odds are against you, can you bear to look slow or cautious to others while you protect what matters and wait for conditions to turn?

tales.title: The Fence at Nagashino
tales.source: Japanese history (Battle of Nagashino, 1575)
tales.tale:
In the summer of 1575 the small castle of Nagashino, held by a young commander named Okudaira Sadamasa and a few hundred men, was surrounded by the army of Takeda Katsuyori. The Takeda were famous across Japan for their cavalry: armoured riders whose charges had shattered army after army in the days of Katsuyori's father, the great Shingen.

The defenders were starving. One of them, Torii Sune'emon, slipped out at night, swam the river past the enemy nets, and ran to seek help from the lords Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu. Help is coming, he was told. He went back to tell his friends, was caught, and was ordered to shout to the castle that no help would come. Instead he shouted the truth, and the Takeda killed him for it.

Help did come, but not the way Katsuyori expected. Nobunaga and Ieyasu did not hurry to the castle walls to fight the Takeda in the open. They halted on the plain of Shitaragahara a few miles away, where a little stream ran across the front of a line of low hills. There their men set to work, not with swords but with axes and spades. They built a long wooden palisade in staggered sections behind the stream, with gaps through which men could sally out. Behind it they placed their foot soldiers with matchlock muskets, thousands of them, and they waited.

Katsuyori's older advisers urged him to withdraw. He chose to attack. On the morning of the battle the Takeda horsemen came on, wave after wave, across the stream and up the muddy slope towards the fence. The muskets fired. Horses and riders fell in heaps before the stakes. Those who reached the palisade could not get through it, and spearmen came out to meet them. The charges went on for hours, and so did the firing.

By early afternoon the Takeda army was broken, and many of its most famous generals lay dead on the field. Nagashino castle was relieved. Nobunaga's men had done little but build a fence and hold their ground; the Takeda had defeated themselves against it.
tales.lesson: First make yourself impossible to beat; then let a proud opponent spend his strength against you.
tales.why: Nobunaga and Ieyasu "first made themselves unbeatable, then waited for the enemy to become beatable"; theirs was the army that "wins first, then seeks battle", while Katsuyori fought first and looked for a way to win.
tales.living: What fence could you build in advance, so that pressure in your work or life breaks against it rather than against you?

tales.title: The Ditch Before Medina
tales.source: Early Islamic history (Battle of the Trench, 627)
tales.tale:
In the early spring of the year 627 word reached the oasis town of Medina that an army was coming: the Quraysh of Mecca and their allies from many tribes, some ten thousand men with horses and camels, the greatest force Arabia had yet seen. The Muslims of Medina could muster perhaps three thousand. To meet such a host in the open plain would be to die there.

The Prophet called a council. Among those present was Salman, a Persian who had travelled a long road from his homeland before coming to Medina. In Persia, he said, when we fear horsemen, we dig a trench.

Medina was already guarded on most sides by lava fields, rocky ground and walled date groves. Only the northern approach lay open. So the whole community took up shovels. In the cold weeks before the enemy arrived they dug a long ditch across that open ground, wide enough that a horse could not leap it and deep enough that a rider could not climb out. The Prophet himself carried earth with the rest. They sang as they worked, and they were hungry.

When the great army arrived, it halted in astonishment. The Arab cavalry had never seen such a thing. Riders galloped up and down the edge looking for a gap; a few daring horsemen forced their way across at a narrow point and were driven back. Arrows flew across the ditch. But no assault could get over it in strength.

The besiegers settled down to wait, and waiting did not suit them. They had brought supplies for a quick victory, not a long stay; their horses ate the forage bare. The alliance began to quarrel, each tribe suspecting the others. Then one night a bitter wind came roaring down from the desert, cold and full of sand. It overturned the cooking pots, blew out the fires and tore the tents loose.

By morning the great army was gone. The Quraysh never again marched against Medina. A ditch dug by tired, hungry people had ended the largest attack they would ever face, and almost no one on either side had died.
tales.lesson: When you are weaker, put your effort into becoming impossible to defeat; a strong enemy who cannot get at you will often defeat himself.
tales.why: Outnumbered, Medina chose that "being unbeatable is a matter of defence" and to "defend when your strength falls short", then waited while the besiegers became beatable through hunger, discord and the weather.
tales.living: When you are outmatched, how could you make yourself hard to hurt rather than trying to win outright?

tales.title: The Race to the Bottom of the World
tales.source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole (1912); history of polar exploration
tales.tale:
In 1911 two expeditions set out across the Antarctic ice towards the South Pole, a place no human being had ever stood. One was led by the British naval officer Robert Falcon Scott, the other by the Norwegian Roald Amundsen.

Amundsen had spent his whole life preparing for this kind of journey. As a young man he had sailed through the Northwest Passage and spent two winters with the Netsilik Inuit, learning how they dressed in loose furs, how they drove dogs, how they travelled without sweating in the cold. He took nothing on trust. He measured the distances, estimated the food each man and dog would need each day, counted the depots, weighed every load.

His answer was dogs: nearly a hundred of them, driven by expert skiers, and a hard plan that some of the dogs would be killed along the way to feed the others. Scott put his faith in a mix of motor sledges, Siberian ponies and, in the end, men hauling the sledges themselves.

Before the winter darkness, Amundsen's men laid depots of food far to the south. Knowing how easy it was to miss a small cairn on the endless white, he marked each depot not with one flag but with a line of flags stretching miles to either side, so that a party slightly off course would cross the line and follow it home.

When the light returned the Norwegians set out. They climbed a great glacier to the polar plateau, slaughtered dogs as planned, and pressed on. On 14 December 1911 they reached the Pole, pitched a tent, planted their flag and left a letter for Scott. Then they turned for home, and they came back to their base fit and well fed, on schedule.

Scott's party reached the Pole five weeks later and found the Norwegian tent. On the way back, short of fuel and food, hammered by cold, all five men died, the last of them only eleven miles from a great store of supplies.

Amundsen's journey had almost no drama in it, which was exactly the point. Victory, he wrote, awaits the one who has everything in order: luck, people call it.
tales.lesson: The surest victories look dull from outside because the hard work was done in the measuring and preparing, before the contest began.
tales.why: Amundsen followed Sunzi's chain, "first, measure; second, estimate; third, count; fourth, weigh", so his triumph brought "no fame for wisdom, no merit for courage": it simply could not go wrong.
tales.living: What contest ahead of you could you turn from a test of nerve into a matter of measuring, counting and preparing?

tales.title: The Vanishing Campfires
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
Thirteen years after the race of the three horses, Sun Bin and his old classmate Pang Juan met again across a war. It was Pang Juan who had once had Sun Bin mutilated out of envy, and now he led the army of Wei.

Qi marched into Wei's land. Pang Juan turned back from another campaign and came after them in fury. The men of Wei had always boasted that the soldiers of Qi were cowards, and Sun Bin knew it.

"Let them believe it," he said to General Tian Ji. "Tonight, have the men dig cooking hearths for a hundred thousand. Tomorrow night, for fifty thousand. The night after, for thirty thousand."

So the army of Qi retreated, and each evening it left behind fewer blackened fire pits in the earth. Pang Juan's scouts counted them, and Pang Juan rode among the ashes, delighted. "I knew it," he said. "Three days in our country and more than half their men have run away."

He left his heavy infantry and baggage behind. With only his swiftest troops he raced ahead, marching day and night, to catch the deserting rabble before it escaped.

Sun Bin reckoned the pace of the pursuit and chose his place: Maling, where the road ran through a narrow pass between steep banks, thick with trees. He had a great tree stripped of its bark, and on the pale wood he wrote a single line. Then he hid ten thousand crossbowmen along the slopes with one order: "When you see a fire lit at dusk, shoot at it."

Pang Juan reached the pass after dark. Something white glimmered on a tree beside the road. He called for a torch and held it up to read the words.

They said: Pang Juan dies beneath this tree.

Before he could finish reading, the slopes erupted. Ten thousand bolts flew towards the light in his hand. The army of Wei broke apart in the darkness, and Pang Juan, seeing that all was lost, took his own life. It is said his last words were bitter: "So I have made that boy famous."
tales.lesson: People believe what they already want to believe. Feed a rival's assumptions with a little evidence and he will hurry himself into your hands.
tales.why: Sun Bin "shows a form, and the enemy follows it": shrinking fires that confirmed Pang Juan's contempt, and then "with his troops he waits for them" at Maling. The pursuit itself tired the enemy, as in "if he is rested, tire him".
tales.living: What story about you does a competitor, colleague or even a family member already believe, and how might that belief be leading them, or you, astray?

tales.title: The Bending Line at Cannae
tales.source: Polybius and Livy (Battle of Cannae, 216 BC)
tales.tale:
On a scorching August morning in southern Italy, beside the river Aufidus, the largest army Rome had ever sent into one field drew itself up for battle. Eight legions and their allies, perhaps eighty thousand men, packed into a deep, heavy block. The plan was as plain as a hammer: march forward, crush the centre, finish the war.

Facing them stood Hannibal of Carthage, far from home, with fewer men and a patchwork army of Africans, Spaniards and Gauls who did not share a language.

Hannibal did something strange with his centre. He set his Gauls and Spaniards out in a long curve that bulged towards the Romans, like a bow bent the wrong way. Behind each end of the curve, out of the line of sight, he placed his veteran African infantry, armed with Roman gear stripped from earlier victories. His cavalry waited on the wings.

The legions surged forward and struck the bulge. It gave way. Step by step the Gauls and Spaniards fell back, fighting hard but yielding ground, and the bulge flattened, then sagged inward into a hollow. The Romans pressed deeper and deeper, crowding into the gap, each rank shoving the one in front, sure that the enemy centre was breaking at last.

It was bending, not breaking. Hannibal himself stood among those retreating men, holding them together.

Then the African veterans on either side simply turned and faced inward. The great Roman mass found spears in its flanks. At the same moment Hannibal's cavalry, which had driven the Roman horsemen from the field, came thundering round and fell upon the rear.

The legions were enclosed on every side. Men were packed so tightly that they could not raise their swords. By evening the field was a slaughterhouse, and one of the two Roman consuls lay among the dead.

For more than two thousand years, generals have studied the morning at Cannae. The Roman plan was not foolish. It was simply the plan everyone expected. Hannibal met it head on, then let it win its way into a trap.
tales.lesson: Meet the expected with the expected, and keep something unexpected in reserve to decide the matter. Apparent retreat can be the most disciplined manoeuvre of all.
tales.why: Hannibal's centre met the Romans in plain combat while the hidden flanks won the day: "join with the orthodox, win with the unexpected". His sagging line seemed like chaos, yet "cannot be thrown into chaos", because its "disorder is born of order".
tales.living: In your current challenge, what is your straightforward, expected move, and what is the surprising move you are holding back to finish it?

tales.title: The Storm at Okehazama
tales.source: Shinchō Kōki (Ōta Gyūichi) and later Japanese accounts
tales.tale:
In the summer of 1560 the great lord Imagawa Yoshimoto marched west with an army so large that the roads groaned under it. Some said twenty thousand men, some said more. His road to Kyoto ran through the small province of Owari, held by a young lord of twenty six named Oda Nobunaga, whom the neighbours called the Fool of Owari. Nobunaga had perhaps two or three thousand soldiers.

The Imagawa vanguard took the Oda border forts of Marune and Washizu in a single morning. Heads were brought to Yoshimoto for inspection, and he was pleased. The day was hot. He ordered his headquarters to halt in a wooded hollow called Dengakuhazama, where his men could rest, eat, drink sake brought by local villagers and sing a little. Owari, it seemed, was already his.

In his castle Nobunaga's councillors begged him to shut the gates and endure a siege. Instead he rose before dawn, sang a verse from the old play Atsumori about the shortness of human life, gulped a bowl of rice standing up and rode out with only a handful of men. Others caught up with him on the road. On a hillside in plain view of the enemy he had banners raised, as though his whole force were camped and waiting there. Then, behind the hill, he led his real army away along the back paths.

Around midday the sky turned black. A summer storm broke over the hills with such violence that, the chronicler says, great trees were thrown down. Rain hammered on helmets and blinded every sentry. Under its cover Nobunaga's men climbed through the dripping woods until they looked down into the hollow where Yoshimoto's camp sat under sodden awnings.

The rain stopped as suddenly as it had begun. In that instant the Oda soldiers poured down the slope with a roar.

The Imagawa thought at first that their own men were brawling. By the time they understood, the attackers were among the curtains of the headquarters. Yoshimoto drew his sword and wounded the first samurai who reached him; the second, Mōri Shinsuke, cut him down. The vast army, still spread for miles along the roads, found itself without a head and melted back toward home.

The Fool of Owari had taken the first step on the road that would make him master of half of Japan.
tales.lesson: Meet the expected with what is expected, then win with what no one is looking for, delivered at the one moment when it cannot be answered.
tales.why: Nobunaga let the enemy see banners where they expected him, then struck from the storm: "join with the orthodox, win with the unexpected." His descent into the hollow was "the swoop of a hawk that breaks its prey", timed to the instant the rain lifted.
tales.living: Where are you doing what everyone expects of you, and what small, well timed move could you add that no one is watching for?

tales.title: The Horns of the Buffalo
tales.source: Historical record (Battle of Isandlwana, 1879)
tales.tale:
Two generations before, the Zulu king Shaka had taken a crowd of clan fighters and given them a shape. Young men were gathered into regiments by age, each with its own name, its own shield colours, its own songs. And every regiment learned one formation, drilled until it ran in the blood. They called it the horns of the buffalo. The chest, the strongest regiments, would meet the enemy face to face. Two horns of younger, swifter men would run wide on either side and curve in to meet behind him. The loins, a reserve of veterans, sat close behind the chest with their backs to the fight, so they would not be tempted to rush in before they were needed.

In January 1879 a British army crossed into Zululand. Its commander, Lord Chelmsford, left a camp of tents and wagons beneath a crouching, lion shaped hill called Isandlwana, and in the dawn of the twenty second he rode off with half his force to chase a Zulu army he believed lay to the east.

It did not. More than twenty thousand warriors were sitting in perfect silence in the folds of the Ngwebeni valley, a few miles from the camp, waiting for a day the elders thought propitious. At midday a party of British horsemen chasing a few herdsmen rode up to the lip of the valley and looked down on the whole army.

A surprise like that might have scattered any other host. It did not scatter this one. Within minutes the regiments rose, found their places and poured out across the plain, and the old shape unfolded as if on a drill ground. The chest came straight at the camp and lay down under the rifle fire, pinning the defenders in place. The left horn swept along the plain. The right horn ran a long way round, out of sight behind the hill itself, and came in on the rear of the camp where no one had thought to look.

That afternoon, while the sun was dimmed by an eclipse, the horns closed. Around 1,300 of the camp's defenders died, and it was the heaviest defeat a modern British army had ever suffered at the hands of an African one.

Chelmsford rode back at nightfall to find his tents slashed and empty, and the impi gone.
tales.lesson: An organisation that has been given a clear shape, with named parts and a shared drill, keeps its form even when it is surprised; a large force without that shape can be cut apart.
tales.why: Shaka's named regiments let twenty thousand fight as one: "to fight with many as you fight with few is a matter of signals, form and name." Even when discovered too early the impi held together, because "order or disorder rests on organisation".
tales.living: If your team, household or week were suddenly thrown into confusion, what shared structure would let everyone still know their place?

tales.title: Nine Days of Running
tales.source: Novgorod First Chronicle; Ibn al-Athir, The Complete History
tales.tale:
In 1223 two of Genghis Khan's generals, Jebe the Arrow and old Subutai, rode north of the Caucasus on a long reconnaissance. They had perhaps twenty thousand horsemen and were thousands of miles from home. On the steppe they fell upon the Cuman nomads, and the Cuman khan Köten fled to his son in law, Mstislav the Bold of Galich, one of the princes of the Rus'. "Today they have taken our land," he told the princes. "Tomorrow they will take yours."

The princes gathered a great host from Kiev, Galich, Chernigov and a dozen smaller towns, and marched down the Dnieper with the Cumans. Mongol envoys came to say they had no quarrel with the Rus'. The princes had them killed.

Then the Mongols did a strange thing. When the Rus' vanguard crossed the river and struck a Mongol rearguard, it broke and ran, and the princes took prisoners and cattle. The main Mongol army fell back eastward across the steppe. The Rus' followed. Each day the enemy was a little ahead, drifting away like smoke, leaving tracks and the odd straggler to be caught. Each day the princes grew surer they had frightened the invaders off. Each day their columns stretched further apart, for the princes were jealous rivals and none would wait for another. For nine days, the accounts say, they chased.

On the last day of May they reached a small river called the Kalka. Mstislav the Bold, eager to win the glory alone, crossed with his own men and the Cumans without telling the prince of Kiev, who was making camp some way behind.

On the far side the steppe was suddenly full of horsemen. The Mongols had stopped running. Their arrows fell in clouds; their armoured lancers came in where the arrows had done their work. The Cumans broke first and fled back through the Rus' lines, trampling their camps. Mstislav the Bold escaped across the river and cut the boats loose behind him. The prince of Kiev, left on a hill behind a ring of wagons, held out for three days and then surrendered on a promise of safety, which was not kept.

Only a fraction of the host came home. And then the Mongols, as quietly as they had come, rode back into the east. They would return fourteen years later.
tales.lesson: Show an opponent a picture he wants to believe, and he will follow it wherever you lead; the eager pursuer is the easiest to ambush.
tales.why: The retreat was a form shown to the princes: "shows a form, and the enemy follows it; offers something, and the enemy takes it." The princes broke the plain rule "do not follow a feigned flight".
tales.living: When someone or something seems to be giving way easily before you, how could you check whether you are being drawn somewhere?

tales.title: Besiege Wei to Rescue Zhao
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
The armies of Wei had surrounded Handan, the capital of Zhao. Every day the siege engines crept closer to the walls, and every day the people of Zhao grew hungrier. At last the king of Zhao sent riders to Qi, begging for help.

The king of Qi agreed. He gave the command to General Tian Ji, with the crippled strategist Sun Bin riding beside him in a covered cart, since he could not sit a horse.

Tian Ji knew what rescue looked like. You marched to the besieged city, you hurled your army against the besiegers, and you drove them away. He gave orders to make for Handan.

Sun Bin stopped him. "When you untangle a knotted skein of silk," he said, "you do not yank at it with your fist. When you separate two men in a fight, you do not join in throwing punches. Strike where they are strong, and you will only add your bodies to the heap."

"Then where?"

"Wei has sent all its best soldiers to Handan. The ones left at home are the old and the weak. March on Daliang, their own capital. Seize the roads, threaten the city. The general of Wei will have to drop everything and run home. Then the siege of Handan lifts itself, and his army wears itself out on the way back to us."

So Qi turned away from Handan, the city it had come to save, and marched straight into the heart of Wei.

The news reached the Wei camp like a thunderclap. Their capital in danger, their families exposed, the generals of Wei abandoned the siege they had fought so long to tighten. They drove their men home at the double, through dust and heat, day after day.

At Guiling, on the road back, the army of Qi was waiting for them, fresh and in position. The weary columns of Wei stumbled into the trap and were broken.

Handan was saved, and not one soldier of Qi had fought beneath its walls.

The Chinese still use the phrase, four characters long, for any clever indirect solution: besiege Wei to rescue Zhao.
tales.lesson: The direct route to a goal is often the most costly. Find the thing your opponent must protect, press on it, and the problem you cared about may untangle itself.
tales.why: Sun Bin made Wei come out because "I strike what he must save", and he aimed at Daliang because to take what you attack you "attack what is not defended".
tales.living: Which problem are you tugging at directly, like a knot, when pressing gently somewhere else might loosen it?

tales.title: The Message in the Night
tales.source: Herodotus, Histories
tales.tale:
In the autumn of 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes had burnt Athens. His fleet, hundreds upon hundreds of ships, lay along the coast, and the Greek fleet sheltered in the narrow strait behind the island of Salamis. The Greek captains quarrelled day and night. Many wanted to slip away south and defend their own homes.

The Athenian commander Themistocles knew that if the fleet scattered, each city would be crushed in turn. And he knew that in the open sea the Persian numbers would swallow them. Only in the narrows could a small fleet face a great one.

So he did something astonishing. He called a trusted slave named Sicinnus, the tutor of his children, and sent him across the water in a small boat to the Persian camp with a message for the king. Themistocles, said Sicinnus, secretly favoured Persia. The Greeks were terrified and quarrelling and would flee in the night. Strike now, block the exits, and the whole Greek fleet is yours.

Xerxes believed it. It was what he hoped to hear. That night he ordered his ships to seal both ends of the strait, and his crews rowed and kept watch through the dark hours, waiting for a Greek escape that never came.

At dawn the Greeks, who had slept, launched their ships, singing their battle hymn. Xerxes had a throne set up on the slopes of the mainland, so that he could watch his victory.

He watched instead as his tired crews crowded into the channel. The huge fleet could not spread out; ships fouled one another, oars snapped, the ranks behind pushed the ranks in front onto Greek rams. In the narrow water, numbers became a burden. The heavy Greek triremes struck again and again at whatever ship was nearest.

By evening the strait was filled with wreckage, and the king who had come to conquer Greece was soon on his way back to Asia.
tales.lesson: Choose the ground and the hour, then persuade your opponent to come to you there. A rested few in the right place can overcome a weary many in the wrong one.
tales.why: Themistocles' message showed Xerxes gain, so the Persians came to battle "worn out" after a sleepless night while the Greeks waited "at ease"; in the narrows the Greeks were concentrated and "many where he is few".
tales.living: Where could you choose the setting of your next difficult conversation or negotiation, rather than meeting it on someone else's terms?

tales.title: Five Smooth Stones
tales.source: The Bible, 1 Samuel 17
tales.tale:
In the valley of Elah two armies faced each other across a stream: the Israelites on one slope, the Philistines on the other. Neither side would come down.

Every morning and every evening, for forty days, a champion walked out from the Philistine ranks. His name was Goliath, of the city of Gath. He stood, the story says, six cubits and a span. His bronze helmet gleamed, his coat of scale armour weighed as much as a grown man, and the iron head of his spear was as heavy as a blacksmith's anvil. A shield bearer walked before him. "Choose a man," he roared. "Let him come down and fight me. If he kills me, we will be your servants."

No one went. King Saul and all his soldiers stood and trembled.

Then a shepherd boy named David arrived with bread and cheese for his older brothers. He heard the challenge and was astonished that no one answered it. His brothers told him to go home. But the words reached the king, and David was brought before him. "I have kept my father's sheep," said the boy, "and I have killed the lion and the bear that came for them."

Saul dressed him in his own armour and set a bronze helmet on his head and hung his sword at his side. David took a few steps, clanking. "I cannot go with these," he said. "I am not used to them." He took them all off.

He went down to the stream with his staff and his sling, and chose five smooth stones from the water, and put them in his shepherd's bag.

Goliath saw a ruddy boy coming at him with a stick and laughed. "Am I a dog?" He lumbered forward, waiting for the clash of close combat, which is how champions fought.

David did not close with him. He ran, and as he ran he slipped a stone into the sling and whirled it once. The stone flew across the gap and struck the giant in the one place his armour did not cover. It sank into his forehead, and Goliath fell on his face in the dust.
tales.lesson: Do not fight your opponent's fight. Refuse the borrowed armour of how things are usually done, and strike where the strength is absent.
tales.why: David would not meet bronze with bronze; like water he "avoids the full and strikes the empty", attacking "what is not defended" on a giant armoured everywhere but one spot.
tales.living: Whose armour are you wearing because it is expected, and what would you do instead if you fought with your own sling?

tales.title: Against the Ropes in Kinshasa
tales.source: Historical record (the 'Rumble in the Jungle', Kinshasa, 1974)
tales.tale:
In the small hours of 30 October 1974, in a football stadium in Kinshasa, Zaire, Muhammad Ali climbed into the ring to face the heavyweight champion of the world. George Foreman was twenty five, unbeaten in forty fights, and had knocked out almost all of them. He had flattened the two men who had beaten Ali, Joe Frazier and Ken Norton, in two rounds apiece. Ali was thirty two. Many ringside writers feared not that he would lose but that he would be badly hurt.

Ali had spent weeks telling the world exactly how he would win. He would dance, as he had in his youth. He would float around the ring until the big slow champion was dizzy from chasing him. The crowd, sixty thousand strong, had taken him to their hearts, and they chanted in Lingala: "Ali, bomaye!"

The first round went more or less to plan. Then, in the second, Ali stopped dancing. To the horror of his own corner, he backed onto the ropes, leaned far back over them, raised his gloves around his head, tucked his elbows into his ribs and let Foreman hit him.

And Foreman did. He hit him round after round, enormous swinging blows to the body and arms, the punches that had ended forty fights. The ropes gave and took some of their force. Ali's forearms took most of the rest. And between the blows, Ali leaned close and talked. "Is that all you got, George? They told me you could punch."

The heat in the stadium was heavy and wet. Foreman, who was used to fights that lasted a few minutes, began to slow. By the sixth round his punches were arriving like tired men climbing stairs. By the seventh he was pawing. Ali, who had spent the night leaning and waiting, was breathing easily.

Late in the eighth round, as Foreman lurched forward once more, Ali came off the ropes. A flurry of quick punches, a left, a right to the head, and the champion spun slowly and went down. He did not beat the count.

Ali later gave his tactic a name: the rope a dope.
tales.lesson: Let the opponent spend his strength on what costs you little; the one who is rested chooses the moment, and the one who is spent cannot answer it.
tales.why: Ali made Foreman come to him and wear himself out: "bring others to them and are not brought." Foreman was strong and fresh, so Ali applied the rule "if he is rested, tire him".
tales.living: In a dispute or long project, are you spending your energy where it counts, or letting someone else set the pace until you are exhausted?

tales.title: The Oar and the Scabbard
tales.source: Japanese legend (later accounts of Miyamoto Musashi)
tales.tale:
In the spring of 1612, two swordsmen agreed to settle which of them was the greater on a tiny island in the strait between Honshu and Kyushu. One was Sasaki Kojirō, famous for a long blade called the Drying Pole and for a cut so swift it was likened to a swallow turning in flight. The other was a young wanderer named Miyamoto Musashi.

The hour was set for the morning. Kojirō arrived on time, splendidly dressed, his great sword at his back. Officials and witnesses gathered on the sand. They waited.

Musashi did not come.

The sun climbed. An hour passed, then another. Messengers were sent across the water to find him, and returned to say he had been asleep. Kojirō paced the shore. The witnesses murmured. His fine composure began to fray.

Meanwhile Musashi sat in the stern of a small boat, unhurried. On the way over, it is said, he took a spare oar and carved it with his short sword into a wooden blade, longer than Kojirō's famous steel. He tied back his sleeves with a strip of paper cord and wrapped a towel round his head.

When at last the boat grounded in the shallows and Musashi stepped into the surf, Kojirō could bear it no longer. He drew his sword and flung the empty scabbard into the waves.

Musashi stood in the water and looked at him. "Kojirō," he said, "you have lost already. Would a man who meant to win throw away his scabbard?"

Rage flooded Kojirō's face. He rushed forward. Behind Musashi the morning sun glittered on the sea, straight into his opponent's eyes.

The two blades moved almost together. Kojirō's cut sliced the towel from Musashi's brow. Musashi's oar came down on Kojirō's head. The famous swordsman fell to the sand and did not rise.

Musashi bowed to the officials, walked back through the shallows to his boat, and was rowed away.

Whether every detail is true no one can say; the story was told and retold long afterwards. But the island has been called Ganryūjima, after Kojirō's school, ever since.
tales.lesson: Spirit is a resource that can be spent, and a long wait in the heat of expectation spends it fast. Keep your own calm, and let impatience do its work on the other side.
tales.why: Musashi struck when Kojirō's "morning spirit" had soured to fretting and anger, a general "robbed of his heart"; he was "quiet" and awaited "the clamour".
tales.living: When you are kept waiting, by a reply, a decision or a rival, what does the waiting do to your judgement, and how could you protect it?

tales.title: Three Hundred Torches
tales.source: The Bible, Judges 7
tales.tale:
The Midianites came up into the land each harvest like locusts, with camels beyond counting, and stripped the fields bare. Against them a farmer named Gideon gathered an army of thirty two thousand men.

Too many, said the voice he trusted. "Whoever is fearful, let him go home." Twenty two thousand went. Still too many. Gideon brought the ten thousand down to the water to drink. Most knelt and put their faces to the stream. Three hundred scooped the water up in their hands and lapped it, eyes up. Those three hundred he kept; the rest he sent away.

That night Gideon crept down with his servant to the edge of the enemy camp, which filled the valley. In the darkness he overheard a Midianite telling his friend a dream: a loaf of barley bread had come tumbling into the camp and knocked a tent flat.
