"That can only be the sword of Gideon," the friend whispered. Gideon understood that the enemy was already afraid.

He went back and gave each of his three hundred men three things: a ram's horn trumpet, an empty clay jar, and a burning torch hidden inside the jar. He split them into three companies and spread them round the sleeping camp on the hills.

"Watch me," he said. "Do what I do."

They waited until the start of the middle watch, just after the guards had been changed and the new sentries were settling to their posts. Then Gideon raised his trumpet and blew.

Three hundred trumpets blared from three sides at once. Three hundred jars smashed together, and three hundred torches blazed out of the dark. Three hundred voices roared: "The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon!"

In the camp, men woke to a ring of fire and a wall of noise. Every torch, they thought, must mean a company; every horn, a regiment. They ran, they collided, and in the black confusion they turned their swords on one another. The great host fled down the valley towards the Jordan, and the three hundred never even had to charge.
tales.lesson: Signals do more than coordinate your own side; they shape what the other side believes it is facing. A small, united band with one rhythm can feel like an army.
tales.why: Gideon's night attack used "many gongs and drums": horns, smashing jars and fire, so "the ears and eyes of men are worked upon"; his men moved as one because signals "make the ears and eyes of the people one".
tales.living: How do you signal to your team, family or audience, and are your signals clear and shared enough to make a few people act as one?

tales.title: The Plum Grove Over the Hill
tales.source: A New Account of Tales of the World (Shishuo Xinyu)
tales.tale:
In the late years of the Han dynasty, the warlord Cao Cao was leading his army along a strange road in the heat of summer. Somewhere they had taken a wrong turn. The guides argued; the map was no help. The wells they had counted on were dry.

By noon the soldiers were parched. Tongues stuck to the roofs of mouths. Men leaned on their spears and stopped. Some sat down at the roadside and would not get up. The column, miles long, began to slow and sag like a rope going slack. An army that stops on a strange road in the heat may not start again.

Cao Cao rode up and down the line. He saw the dull eyes and the cracked lips. He had no water to give them, and he did not know where water was.

Then he stood in his stirrups, pointed down the road towards a far ridge, and called out in a great voice.

"Just over that hill there is a big plum grove! The trees are loaded with fruit. Sweet plums and sour plums, enough for everyone. They will quench your thirst!"

The word ran down the line from man to man. Plums. Sour plums. And at the very thought of biting into one, the soldiers' mouths began to water. Their dry throats eased a little. They picked up their spears and fell back into step, quickening as they went, each man thinking of the fruit, the shade, the juice running down his chin.

They marched over the ridge. There was no plum grove.

But they kept going, and the next ridge led them down to a stream, and the whole army knelt along its banks and drank.

The story became a Chinese proverb: to gaze at plums to quench a thirst. People sometimes use it to mock empty comfort. Yet on that road, on that day, the thought of plums was enough to carry thousands of men to real water.
tales.lesson: The spirit of a group can be lost to weariness long before its strength is gone; give people something vivid to march towards, and you can carry them through the gap.
tales.why: Cao Cao saw his army's spirit flagging, for "a whole army can be robbed of its spirit", and restored it with a single image, a small instance of making "misfortune" into "gain" on a winding road.
tales.living: When your team, or you alone, are running dry halfway through a long task, what picture of the destination could renew the will to keep moving?

tales.title: The Long Way Round the Island
tales.source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, Book V
tales.tale:
In the spring of 326 BC Alexander of Macedon came to the river Hydaspes, in the Punjab, and found the far bank lined with an army. King Porus stood there with his infantry, his chariots and some two hundred war elephants. The monsoon rains had begun, and the river ran wide, brown and fast. No horse would face an elephant across it, and no army could cross under arrows in water that deep.

So Alexander did nothing, loudly. He had grain brought in from all over the country, so that Porus's scouts would report he meant to wait until the river fell in winter. Night after night his cavalry rode up and down the bank with shouting, war cries and trumpets, as if about to cross. Each time Porus led his elephants along the far shore to meet them. Each time nothing happened. After a while Porus stopped bothering, and simply posted watchmen along the river.

Some seventeen miles upstream, Alexander's scouts had found a place where the river bent around a wooded headland, with an island in midstream that would hide boats from the far bank. There he had boats and rafts made of stuffed hides secretly gathered.

He left his general Craterus in the main camp with a large force, in plain sight of Porus, with orders not to cross unless Porus moved his elephants away. A man who looked like Alexander, the story goes, wore the king's armour in the royal tent. Then, one night, under a crashing thunderstorm that drowned the noise of arms and orders, Alexander marched the long way round, upstream through the darkness and rain.

At dawn they crossed behind the island. They landed, only to find they were on another island, cut off by a channel that had swollen in the night. They waded the last stretch with the water at their chests.

By the time Porus learned of it, Alexander's cavalry was on his side of the river. He turned to fight on ground he had not chosen, and lost. Brought to Alexander wounded, and asked how he wished to be treated, Porus said only: "Like a king." Alexander gave him back his kingdom.
tales.lesson: The shortest road on the map is often the longest in fact; taking the roundabout path, while the other side watches the obvious one, can get you there first.
tales.why: Alexander marched seventeen miles to cross a few hundred yards of river: "lengthen your own route ... set out after him, arrive before him." His noisy feints kept him "unreadable as shadow" until the crossing came "in motion, a clap of thunder".
tales.living: Where are you pushing straight at a guarded front door, when a longer, quieter route might get you there sooner?

tales.title: The Gift of a Woman's Headdress
tales.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms (Chen Shou) and Book of Jin
tales.tale:
In the year 234, the great strategist Zhuge Liang of Shu marched north for the last time and camped on the Wuzhang Plains, south of the river Wei. Opposite him, in a fortified camp, sat Sima Yi, commander of the armies of Wei.

Zhuge Liang wanted a battle. His supplies came over terrible mountain roads, and he could not wait for ever. Sima Yi knew it, and would not come out.

Weeks passed. Zhuge Liang tried every challenge. Then he sent an envoy across with a gift for Sima Yi: a woman's headdress and women's clothes. The meaning was plain to every soldier. A man who hides behind his walls is no man at all.

Sima Yi's officers were beside themselves. Their honour, the army's honour, had been mocked in front of the whole world. They crowded into his tent and demanded to fight.

Sima Yi did not seem angry. He sent a formal request to the emperor in Luoyang, asking permission to attack. The emperor understood exactly what was wanted. He sent back an old and stern minister, Xin Pi, carrying the staff of imperial authority, who stood at the gate of the camp and forbade anyone to march out. The officers grumbled, and obeyed.

On the other side, one of Zhuge Liang's men said: "Sima Yi will not come now." Zhuge Liang replied that Sima Yi had never meant to fight; asking the emperor was only a way of calming his own men.

Meanwhile, Sima Yi had quietly asked Zhuge Liang's envoy a few friendly questions. Not about the army, only about the chancellor's habits. How did he sleep? How much did he eat? The envoy answered proudly: his master rose early and went to bed late, ate only a little, and reviewed in person every punishment of twenty strokes or more.

When the envoy had gone, Sima Yi said: "He eats little and works too much. How can he last long?"

That autumn, Zhuge Liang fell ill in his camp and died. The army of Shu withdrew into the mountains, and Sima Yi had won without a battle.
tales.lesson: An insult is an invitation to act on someone else's timetable. Keep your position strong, let your pride take the blow, and watch what your opponent cannot sustain.
tales.why: Zhuge Liang aimed at the danger of the general "jealous of his honour", who "can be shamed"; Sima Yi declined, and trusted "in having made yourself unassailable" behind his walls.
tales.living: What taunt, criticism or provocation is currently tempting you to act sooner or louder than your own plan calls for?

tales.title: The Lion in the Well
tales.source: Indian folk tale (Panchatantra)
tales.tale:
In a forest there lived a lion called Bhasuraka, so strong and so greedy that he killed far more animals each day than he could ever eat. The deer, the boar, the buffalo and the hare met together in fear. At last they went to him with a bargain. "Lord, stay in your den. Each day we will send you one animal to eat. Then you will never go hungry, and we will not all be destroyed." The lion agreed, but he warned them: if a single day's meal ever failed to come, he would kill them all.

So it went, day after day, until the lot fell upon a small hare.

The hare walked to the den very slowly. He dawdled by streams. He nibbled clover. He lay in the shade and thought. When at last he came before the lion, the sun was low, and Bhasuraka was roaring with hunger and rage.

"You speck of fur! You are late, and you are small. I will eat you, and then I will kill every beast in the forest."

The hare bowed low. "Lord, it was not my fault. The animals sent five hares with me, knowing I was too small to be a meal. But on the way another lion leapt out of a hole in the ground and seized the other four. I told him they belonged to you, King Bhasuraka. He laughed and said that this forest was his, and you were a thief. He sent me to tell you so."

The lion's mane bristled. "Another king in my forest? Show me this upstart. Now!"

The hare led him to an old well, deep and round, full of dark water. "He lives down there, lord. He has gone back into his fortress."

Bhasuraka peered over the edge. In the water a great lion glared up at him, mane bristling, teeth bared. Bhasuraka roared, and from the well a roar came back, louder.

Mad with fury, the lion hurled himself down at his enemy.

The hare went home, and the animals of the forest lived in peace.
tales.lesson: Anger makes even the strongest predictable. Whoever can be provoked can be led, and the provoker need not be strong at all.
tales.why: The lion was "quick to anger" and so "can be goaded by insult", one of the five dangers that, as the next verse says, are "the ruin of any campaign".
tales.living: Who in your life, or what kind of situation, can reliably make you angry, and what might someone steer you into by using it?

tales.title: The Oak and the Reed
tales.source: Aesop
tales.tale:
On the bank of a river stood an oak tree that had stood there for three hundred years. Its trunk was as thick as a cottage, and its roots went down into the bank like the fingers of a great hand. Birds nested in it, cattle rested under it, and travellers steered their boats by it. Each spring it grew a little broader, and each spring it grew a little prouder.

At its foot, in the shallows, grew a bed of reeds. They were thin and pale and they never stood still. When a duck paddled past, they wavered. When a breeze crossed the water, they bowed all together, like a crowd greeting a king.

"How sad to be you," said the oak one calm evening. "The least wind pushes you about. A sparrow landing on you would bend you double. Look at me. I stand straight in all weathers. I bow to nothing."

The reeds rustled. "We are content," they said. "We bend, but we do not break."

That night a storm came off the hills, the worst in living memory. The wind screamed down the valley. Rain came sideways. The river rose and roared.

The reeds lay down flat upon the water, as low as they could go, and let the gale pour over them. They bent this way and that, they were flung and tossed, but they held on by their roots and gave way to every gust.

The oak stood firm. It set its great branches against the wind, and the wind pushed. The oak pushed back. Branches cracked and flew away into the dark, but still it would not bow. The wind pushed harder.

Towards dawn there came a sound like a cannon. The ground split. The great roots tore out of the bank, and the oak toppled across the river and lay there with its crown in the water.

In the morning the sky was clear and the river was quiet. The reeds stood up again, one by one, dripping and swaying in the sunlight, and looked at the fallen giant lying among them.
tales.lesson: Strength that cannot change its shape is brittle. The ability to yield, adapt and rise again often outlasts power that only knows how to stand firm.
tales.why: The oak knew only one way to stand, like the general who "may know the lie of the land and still win nothing from it" without "the art of variation"; the reeds knew there is "ground not to be contested".
tales.living: Where are you holding a position out of pride when bending for a season would let you stand again tomorrow?

tales.title: Brer Rabbit and the Tar-Baby
tales.source: African American folk tale (recorded by Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
tales.tale:
Brer Fox had chased Brer Rabbit for years and never once caught him. So one day he mixed up a great lump of sticky tar and turpentine, shaped it into a little figure with a round head and a hat on top, and set it by the side of the big road. Then he lay down in the bushes to watch.

Before long Brer Rabbit came along, lippity clippity, as pert as a jaybird. He saw the little figure sitting there and stopped.

"Good morning!" says Brer Rabbit. "Fine weather we're having."

The Tar-Baby said nothing. Brer Fox lay low.

"How are you feeling this morning?" says Brer Rabbit. The Tar-Baby said nothing.

"Are you deaf?" says Brer Rabbit. "Because if you are, I can holler louder." The Tar-Baby said nothing.

Now Brer Rabbit began to swell up. "You're stuck up, that's what you are," he says. "I'll teach you how to speak to respectable folk. If you don't take off that hat and say howdy, I'm going to bust you wide open."

The Tar-Baby said nothing. So Brer Rabbit drew back his fist and hit it on the side of the head. His fist stuck fast. "Let me go or I'll hit you again!" He hit it with the other fist, and that stuck too. He kicked it, and his foot stuck. He kicked with the other foot, and finally butted it with his head, and there he was, stuck all over, while Brer Fox strolled out of the bushes laughing fit to burst.

"Well now, Brer Rabbit," says Brer Fox. "This time I reckon I'll have you for my dinner."

Brer Rabbit spoke very humbly. "Do what you like with me, Brer Fox. Roast me, hang me, drown me. But whatever you do, please don't fling me in that briar patch."

Brer Fox wanted to hurt him as badly as he could. So he unstuck him from the tar, swung him round by the hind legs and flung him into the middle of the briar patch.

There was a great crashing. Then, from up on the hill, a voice called out. Brer Rabbit was sitting cross legged on a log, combing the tar out of his fur with a chip. "I was bred and born in a briar patch, Brer Fox!" he cried, and away he went.
tales.lesson: Pride that must answer every slight can be trapped by anything that refuses to answer; and a mind that turns trouble over can find the advantage hidden inside it.
tales.why: Brer Rabbit is caught by his own wounded honour, the general who is "quick to anger" and "can be goaded by insult". Then, stuck fast, he finds the gain within the harm: "mingle gain into thoughts of harm, and trouble can be untied."
tales.living: What "tar-baby" in your life, a rude message, a silent colleague, a slight online, keeps tempting you to hit back until you are stuck?

tales.title: The Wall at Hakata Bay
tales.source: Japanese chronicles; the Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba scrolls of Takezaki Suenaga
tales.tale:
In the autumn of 1274 a fleet sent by Kublai Khan, ruler of the Mongols and of China, appeared off Hakata Bay in northern Kyushu. Its soldiers came ashore on the beaches and met the samurai of Kyushu, who rode out expecting to fight as they always had, with a challenge and a single combat. Instead they met massed archers, drums, gongs and exploding iron bombs. The Japanese fell back inland. Then the invaders went back to their ships, and a storm scattered the fleet on its way home.

Many in Japan might have taken this as proof that the gods would always protect the islands. The military government at Kamakura, led by the young regent Hōjō Tokimune, took it as a warning. When Kublai's envoys came demanding submission, Tokimune had them beheaded. Everyone understood that the Mongols would return.

So in 1276 the warrior families of Kyushu were ordered to build a wall. Each estate was given a stretch to raise according to the size of its lands. Along some twenty kilometres of the curving shore of Hakata Bay, from Imazu in the west to Kashii in the east, they piled stone and packed earth into a rampart about two metres high, with a steep face to the sea and a gentle slope behind for defenders to climb. Year after year, guards were rotated to man it, and the wall was kept in repair.

In the summer of 1281 the Mongols came again, in far greater numbers: one fleet from Korea and a second, larger one from southern China. When the Korean fleet sailed into Hakata Bay, its captains found the beaches they had used seven years earlier closed by a wall, lined with archers. They could not land in force. They seized the small island of Shikanoshima instead and anchored offshore to wait for the second fleet.

For weeks the invaders lay crowded aboard their ships in the summer heat, while Japanese warriors rowed out in small boats by night to board and burn them. When the southern fleet finally joined them, it was the season of storms. At the end of the summer a typhoon struck the crowded anchorage and destroyed most of the ships.

The wind became famous as the kamikaze, the divine wind. But the wind had found the fleet still at sea because of the wall.
tales.lesson: Do not build your safety on the hope that trouble will not come; build it on preparations that make trouble unable to get in.
tales.why: The Kamakura government did not trust its luck after 1274; it raised a wall: "do not trust that he will not attack; trust in having made yourself unassailable."
tales.living: Which risk in your life, at work, in your health or your money, are you hoping will not arrive, and what wall could you build before it does?

tales.title: Wind and Cranes at the Fei River
tales.source: Book of Jin (Fang Xuanling et al.)
tales.tale:
Fu Jian, ruler of Former Qin, had united the whole of the north and now looked south at the little Jin court beyond the Yangtze. His ministers begged him to wait. He only smiled. "My army is so vast that if every man threw his riding whip into the river, we would dam the current." He marched with a host that the chroniclers numbered in the hundreds of thousands.

The Jin generals, Xie Shi and Xie Xuan, had perhaps eighty thousand. They came up to the Fei River and found the Qin army drawn up thick along the far bank, blocking every ford.

One evening Fu Jian climbed the walls of Shouyang to look at his enemy. The Jin camps were neat and their lines quiet and orderly. Then he looked at the hills of Bagong beyond, where the grass and trees stirred in the wind, and for a moment every bush seemed to him a soldier. He turned to his brother. "These are no weak enemy," he murmured, and for the first time he was afraid.

Next morning a Jin messenger crossed with a strange request. "Your camp hugs the water," said Xie Xuan's letter, "which shows you mean to hold, not to fight. Draw back a little, let us cross, and we will settle this in a single day."

Fu Jian's generals warned him against it. Fu Jian waved them away. "Let them cross. When half are in the water, our cavalry will cut them to pieces." So the order to fall back went out.

But a vast army is a clumsy creature. The front ranks stepped backwards, the ranks behind saw them coming and thought they were fleeing. Then a Jin prisoner in the Qin lines, a man named Zhu Xu, began shouting at the top of his voice: "Qin is beaten! Qin is beaten!" The withdrawal turned into a stampede. Fu Jian's brother, galloping to stop it, fell from his horse and was cut down. The Jin troops splashed across the river and fell upon a mob.

The fugitives ran for days. They slept in the fields, and every time the wind sighed or a crane cried in the night, they jumped up and ran again, sure the Jin were at their heels.
tales.lesson: Numbers are not strength unless they can move as one. A plan that depends on the enemy behaving exactly as you expect can unravel your own side first.
tales.why: Fu Jian meant to strike when "half his force reach the bank," as 9.2 advises, but trusted to sheer size; 9.15 says plainly, "In war, more is not better."
tales.living: Is something you rely on, a big team, a big budget, a big reputation, making you clumsy in the very moment you need to turn quickly?

tales.title: Footprints at the Lion's Cave
tales.source: Aesop
tales.tale:
There was once a lion who had grown too old to run down a gazelle. His teeth were worn, his legs were stiff, and the young antelope laughed at him from a safe distance. Hunger sharpened his wits where age had blunted his claws.

He lay down in the mouth of his cave and began to groan. He let it be known, through the chattering birds who carry every rumour across the plain, that the king of beasts was dying, that he bore no one any grudge, and that he longed to say farewell to each of his subjects before the end.

The animals were touched. A king who asks for nothing but a last goodbye is a sad and gentle thing. First came the goat, bowing low, and he went inside to pay his respects. Then the sheep, then the calf, then a young deer with soft eyes. Each walked into the shadow of the cave, and each was very welcome indeed.

At last the fox came trotting up the path. She did not go in. She sat down a little way off, tail around her feet, and called out politely, "Good morning, Your Majesty. They tell me you are unwell."

"Ah, little fox," sighed the lion from the darkness, "I am very ill. My eyes are dim. Come closer, so I can see your face one last time."

The fox did not move. She was looking at the dust in front of the cave, where the ground was soft and every visitor had left a mark.

"I would come in gladly," she said, "and I am sorry for your trouble. But I notice something curious about your doorway. I see a great many footprints going in. I do not see a single one coming out."

And she turned and trotted home, and lived to be a grey old fox herself.
tales.lesson: Words cost nothing; tracks do not lie. When someone's tender message and the evidence on the ground disagree, believe the ground.
tales.why: The lion's dying wish is a classic case of "Peace asked for with no pledge given: there is a plot," and his invitation onto easy ground, as 9.9 says, "serves some purpose of his."
tales.living: When an offer sounds generous, have you looked at what happened to the last people who accepted it?

tales.title: The General Who Sucked the Wound
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
Wu Qi was a hard man, ambitious and restless, and the stories told against him were many. But when he commanded the armies of Wei against the state of Qin, his soldiers would have followed him anywhere, and the reason was simple to see.

He ate what the lowest foot soldier ate, from the same pot and at the same time. He wore the same rough clothes. At night he did not have a mat laid for him but slept on the bare ground among the men. On the march he refused to ride or be carried; he walked, and he shouldered his own bundle of rations like everyone else. Whatever hardship the ranks endured, the general endured with them, and they watched him do it.

One day a common soldier fell sick with a festering sore. The abscess swelled and would not break, and the man lay in pain. Wu Qi came to him, knelt down, put his mouth to the wound and drew out the poison with his own lips. The whole camp heard of it by nightfall.

When news reached the soldier's village, his mother sat down and wept.

Her neighbours were puzzled. "Your son is only a common soldier," they said, "and the general himself sucked the poison from his wound. Why are you crying? You should be proud."

"You do not understand," she said. "Years ago Lord Wu did the very same for my husband. After that, my husband would not take one step backwards in battle, not one, and so he died facing the enemy. Now Lord Wu has done it for my son. I do not know where my son will die, and that is why I am weeping."

Under Wu Qi, the armies of Wei took five walled cities from Qin, and Qin did not dare march east while he held the frontier.
tales.lesson: People give everything to a leader who shares their hardship rather than merely praising it. That loyalty is real power, and it carries a real weight of responsibility.
tales.why: Wu Qi treated his men "as your beloved sons," and so, as 10.11 promises, "they will stand with you to the death"; the mother's tears show how literally that can come true.
tales.living: Which hardships do you ask of the people around you that you have never shouldered yourself?

tales.title: The Pass at the Hot Gates
tales.source: Herodotus, Histories
tales.tale:
When Xerxes of Persia came down into Greece with an army so large that men said it drank rivers dry, the Greeks looked at their maps and chose a single place to stand. At Thermopylae, the Hot Gates, the road squeezed between steep mountains and the sea, so narrow in places that a cart could barely pass. There, numbers would count for very little.

Leonidas, king of Sparta, arrived first with three hundred Spartans and a few thousand allies. They rebuilt an old wall the Phocians had once raised across the gap and took their stand behind it.

Xerxes waited four days, expecting so small a force to slip away. It did not. On the fifth day he sent in his troops. They came on in waves and were cut down in the narrows, where only a few could fight at once and the long Greek spears outreached them. Then he sent his own guard, the Immortals. They fared no better. The Spartans would turn and run as if beaten, and when the Persians surged after them in disorder, they wheeled about and struck. For two days the pass held.

Then a local man came to the Persian camp. His name was Ephialtes, from Trachis nearby, and he had come for a reward. He knew a goat track that wound up over the mountain and came down behind the Greek position. That night the Immortals followed him through the oak woods by starlight. The Phocians posted to guard the path heard the crunch of dry leaves at dawn, but too late.

Runners brought Leonidas the news. He sent most of the allies home while there was still time. He and his three hundred stayed, and the Thespians stayed beside them, and they fought until there was no one left to fight.

Later the Greeks set a stone on the spot. Its message was short: go tell the Spartans, passer-by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie.
tales.lesson: Narrow ground lets a few hold back many, but only if every way around is known and held. One unwatched path undoes the strongest position.
tales.why: Leonidas did exactly as 10.4 says: "if we are there first, we must fill the pass and wait for the enemy"; Xerxes broke through because, as 11.20 warns, without "local guides" no one can "gain the advantage of the ground."
tales.living: Where is the goat track around your best defences, the one weak point you have not thought to guard?

tales.title: War on Bamboo Slips
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
Zhao Kuo was the son of a great general, and from boyhood he had read every book of war in his father's house. He could recite them, argue them, and win every debate about them. Even his father, Zhao She, could not beat him in an argument about strategy. Yet his father never praised him.

"Why not?" asked Zhao Kuo's mother.

"War is a matter of life and death," said the old general, "and he speaks of it as if it were easy. If Zhao ever makes him a commander, he will destroy our army."

Years later the armies of Qin came against Zhao at a place called Changping. The Zhao commander there was old Lian Po, and he did the wise thing: he built walls, dug in, and refused to come out. Qin was far from home and its supplies were stretched. Month after month Lian Po waited, and the Qin generals fumed.

So Qin sent agents into the Zhao capital with gold and whispers. "Qin is not afraid of Lian Po," the whisper went. "He is old and timid. The only man Qin fears is Zhao Kuo."

The young king believed it. Old Lin Xiangru protested, "Sending Zhao Kuo because of his reputation is like gluing the pegs of a zither and then trying to play a tune. He has read his father's books, but he does not know how to adapt." Zhao Kuo's own mother went to the king and begged him not to appoint her son. The king would not listen.

Zhao Kuo arrived at Changping, threw out Lian Po's arrangements, changed the officers, and led the army out to attack. The Qin general Bai Qi pretended to fall back, drew him on into the hills, then sent horsemen to cut the road behind him and split his army in two. Surrounded, the Zhao troops went hungry for forty-six days. Zhao Kuo led a last charge and was shot dead.

The whole Zhao army surrendered, and the chroniclers say four hundred thousand men were lost.
tales.lesson: Knowledge from books is only half the picture. Without a feel for the real ground and the real enemy, eloquence becomes a danger, not a gift.
tales.why: Zhao Kuo knew the texts but not "the hazards and narrows, the far and the near"; as 10.9 says, "who knows it not and fights will surely lose," whereas 10.13's true knower "moves without confusion."
tales.living: Where are you confident because you have read about something, rather than because you have actually done it?

tales.title: Smash the Pots, Sink the Boats
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
In the last days of the Qin dynasty, the rebel state of Zhao was besieged in the city of Julu by a huge imperial army. Armies from half a dozen other rebel lords came to help, looked at the size of the Qin camps, built themselves sturdy stockades a safe distance away, and sat behind them to watch.

Xiang Yu was a young general from Chu, tall as a door and with a temper to match. His own superior had dawdled on the march for forty-six days, waiting to see which way things would go. Xiang Yu walked into his tent one morning and came out holding the man's head. Then he took the army across the Zhang River himself.

On the far bank, he gave his orders. Sink the boats. Smash the cooking pots. Burn the huts. Every man was to carry three days' rations, and no more.

The soldiers stared at the ripples where the boats went down. There was no road home now, and no meal after the third day. If they wanted to eat again, they would have to eat from the enemy's stores. Every man understood it without a word being said.

They fell on the Qin lines like men who had already died once and were not worried about doing it again. Nine times they met the enemy, and nine times they broke him. They cut the Qin supply road, killed one commander, captured another, and the third burned himself rather than be taken.

All this while the other rebel lords stood on their ramparts and watched. Their men shouted to see it, but did not come out. The noise of the Chu warriors, it was said, shook the sky, and every one of them fought as if he were ten.

When it was over, Xiang Yu summoned the allied generals to his camp. They came in through the gate on their knees, and not one of them dared to raise his eyes to his face.
tales.lesson: When retreat is still possible, part of the mind is always planning it. Remove the way back and all of a person's strength goes forward.
tales.why: Xiang Yu did exactly what 11.17 describes, "burns the boats, smashes the cooking pots"; and, as 11.10 promises, "Soldiers sunk deep in danger lose their fear."
tales.living: What escape route are you quietly keeping open that lets you give only half of yourself to the thing that matters?

tales.title: Over the Roof of the World
tales.source: Polybius and Livy
tales.tale:
Rome ruled the sea. Everyone knew that if the Carthaginians wanted to fight Rome, they would come by ship, and the Roman fleets were ready. One consul sailed for Spain to meet Hannibal there; another prepared to cross to Africa and strike at Carthage itself.

Hannibal did not come by sea. In the spring of 218 BC he marched out of New Carthage in Spain with tens of thousands of foot soldiers, cavalry, and thirty-seven war elephants, and he turned north, towards the mountains no army was supposed to cross.

He fought his way over the Pyrenees. He reached the Rhône, wide and fast, with hostile tribes on the far bank. He sent a column upstream to cross quietly and appear behind them, then floated his elephants over on great rafts heaped with earth so the beasts would think they were still on land. A few panicked and plunged into the river and swam ashore, trunks held high. By the time the Roman consul reached the crossing, Hannibal was three days gone.

Then the Alps. It was late in the year, and the passes were already white. Mountain tribes rolled boulders onto the column from the heights. Horses slid off icy ledges and dragged men with them into the gorges. Hannibal had Gaulish chiefs from the far side guiding him, and he leaned on them at every fork. Near the top, the track was blocked by a landslide of rock. Livy tells that his men felled trees, built huge fires against the stone, poured sour wine onto the hot rock until it cracked, and hacked a road through with their picks.

Fifteen days in the high passes. Perhaps half his army died on the way.

But when the survivors came down into the green plains of northern Italy, the Romans were astonished. The war they had planned to fight in Spain and Africa was now in their own fields, and the enemy was already among the Gauls of the Po, who had hated Rome for years and now flocked to his banners.
tales.lesson: The surest surprise comes by the road everyone else has ruled out. Daring routes demand local knowledge and a willingness to pay a heavy price.
tales.why: Hannibal chose to "go by the road they never imagined" and "strike where they have set no guard," as 11.8 urges, and he leaned on mountain guides because, as 11.20 says, "if you do not use local guides, you cannot gain the advantage of the ground."
tales.living: Which route to your goal have you dismissed as impossible simply because nobody you know has taken it?

tales.title: The Fires of Yiling
tales.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms (Chen Shou)
tales.tale:
Liu Bei and Guan Yu had sworn to be brothers, and for thirty years they had been closer than blood. So when the state of Wu seized the province Guan Yu was holding and put him to death, Liu Bei, now emperor of Shu, could think of nothing but revenge.

His wisest general, Zhao Yun, warned him. "Our true enemy is Wei in the north, not Wu. Strike Wei and Wu will come to heel." Liu Bei would not hear it. Then, as the army prepared to march, his other sworn brother, Zhang Fei, was murdered in his tent by his own officers. Grief upon grief. Liu Bei marched east down the Yangtze with his whole strength.

Wu gave its command to Lu Xun, a young scholar whom the old Wu generals openly despised. Lu Xun studied the Shu army, saw how hot its fury ran, and did nothing. He pulled back, gave up ground, and refused every challenge. The Shu soldiers shouted insults at his walls. His own officers called him a coward behind his back. Lu Xun waited.

Spring passed into summer. The Shu army, tired of baking on the open riverbanks, moved into the cool shade of the forests, and strung its camps out one after another for mile upon mile through the trees, wooden stockades among dry undergrowth.

Then Lu Xun gave his orders. Every soldier was to carry a bundle of dry thatch. On a single night, with the wind behind them, they slipped forward and set the forest alight. Camp after camp went up in flame. More than forty Shu positions burned in the darkness, and Lu Xun's men struck the survivors as they fled the smoke.

Liu Bei escaped up the river to the little fortress of Baidi with a handful of men. Behind him lay his army, his stores, his boats. He never returned home. Within the year he fell ill there and died, having entrusted his young son and his ruined kingdom to the care of his chancellor.
tales.lesson: Anger chooses the fight; wisdom should choose it. Rage makes people careless, and a patient opponent will wait for that carelessness to set the stage.
tales.why: Liu Bei raised his army out of grief and fury, exactly what 12.6 forbids: "A ruler must not raise an army out of anger"; and as 12.7 says, "nor can the dead be brought back to life," not Guan Yu, nor the army that burned for him.
tales.living: What decision are you tempted to make while still hot, that you might need to live with long after the feeling has cooled?

tales.title: The Khan and His Falcon
tales.source: Folk legend (retold in Baldwin's Fifty Famous Stories)
tales.tale:
Genghis Khan rode out to hunt one morning with his friends and his hounds, and on his wrist sat his favourite falcon, a bird he had trained himself and loved better than any horse. All day they rode through the woods, but the game was scarce, and towards evening the others turned for home by the easy road. The Khan, restless, took a shorter path alone through the hills.

The day had been hot, and he was very thirsty. The summer had dried up the streams. At last, beneath a rock, he found a thin trickle of water dripping from above, one slow drop after another. He took the little silver cup from his belt and held it under the drip, and waited a long time while it filled.

He raised the cup to his lips. With a rush of wings the falcon swept off his wrist, struck the cup from his hand, and the water spilled into the dust.

The Khan frowned, picked up the cup, and held it under the drip again. Again he waited. Again, just as it was full, the falcon dived and knocked it flying.

A third time. And a third time the bird struck it down.

"Do that once more," said the Khan quietly, drawing his sword, "and it will be your last." He filled the cup a fourth time. The falcon flew. The sword flashed, and the bird fell dead at his feet.

In his anger he climbed the rock to find the spring itself, so that he could drink without waiting. At the top he found a pool, and lying in it, poisoning every drop, the body of a huge dead snake.

The Khan stood very still for a long while. Then he went down, and gently picked up the falcon, and rode home with it in his arms. He had a figure of the bird made in gold, and on one wing his craftsmen engraved the words: even when a friend does something you do not like, he is still your friend. On the other: whatever is done in anger is done badly.
tales.lesson: Anger acts before it understands. What it destroys often cannot be restored, so the moment of greatest heat is the moment to pause.
tales.why: The Khan's fury passed within minutes, just as 12.7 says "Anger may turn back to gladness," yet the falcon, like the fallen state, could never be "brought back to life."
tales.living: Who in your life keeps knocking the cup from your hand, and have you asked why before deciding they are against you?

tales.title: The Feast Meant for Fan Zeng
tales.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Sima Qian)
tales.tale:
Liu Bang, the future founder of the Han, was penned inside the city of Xingyang, and Xiang Yu's army was squeezing it like a fist. At Xiang Yu's side stood an old adviser named Fan Zeng, sharp as a needle, and Liu Bang feared him more than all the swords of Chu.

His counsellor Chen Ping came to him with an idea. "Xiang Yu is brave, but he is suspicious, and he listens to slander. Give me gold, and let me buy his trust away from him."

Liu Bang gave him forty thousand catties of gold and never once asked how it was spent. Chen Ping sent agents through the Chu camp with purses in their sleeves, spreading whispers: Fan Zeng and the other generals are bitter that they have won so much and received so little; they are talking to Han in secret about dividing the spoils.

Before long, Xiang Yu sent an envoy into Xingyang to sound out the enemy. Chen Ping was ready. The envoy was led into a hall where a magnificent banquet had been laid out: whole roasted ox, the finest wine, dishes on golden stands. Servants bowed low. Then a Han officer looked at the man closely and gave a start.

"Oh! We thought you came from Fan Zeng," he said. "But you are only King Xiang's envoy."

The splendid dishes were carried away. In their place came a bowl of coarse millet and a plate of greens.

The envoy went back to the Chu camp burning with the insult, and told Xiang Yu everything. From that day Xiang Yu doubted Fan Zeng. He began to take away his authority and stopped listening to his advice. Fan Zeng, who had given everything to Chu, saw what had happened.

"The affairs of the world are mostly settled," he said bitterly. "Let my lord handle them himself. I ask leave to take my old bones home." Xiang Yu let him go. Before he reached his home town, an ulcer broke out on his back, and the old man died on the road.

Without him, Xiang Yu made mistake after mistake, and in the end lost everything to Liu Bang.
tales.lesson: Information and trust are worth more than armies, and a little spent on knowing and shaping what the enemy believes can save a fortune in blood.
tales.why: Liu Bang did not "begrudge rank, salary and a hundred pieces of gold" (13.2), and the envoy became an unwitting carrier of "false matters," the method 13.5 calls the doomed agent.
tales.living: When a piece of gossip makes you doubt someone who has served you well, do you ask who benefits from your doubting them?

tales.title: The Scarlet Cord of Jericho
tales.source: Hebrew Bible, Book of Joshua
tales.tale:
Before Joshua led the tribes of Israel across the Jordan, he did not consult the stars. He chose two young men, gave them a quiet word, and sent them across the river to look at Jericho with their own eyes.

They slipped into the city and found lodging in the house of a woman named Rahab. Her house was built into the city wall itself, and travellers came and went from it without much notice. But somebody noticed. Before nightfall word reached the king of Jericho that Israelite spies had entered the city, and his soldiers came hammering at Rahab's door.

"Bring out the men who came to you," they demanded.

Rahab had already taken the two up to her flat roof and hidden them beneath the stalks of flax she had laid out to dry in the sun. "Yes, some men came," she told the soldiers easily, "but I did not know where they were from. They left at dusk, just before the gate was shut. Hurry, and you may still catch them." And the king's men hurried off down the road towards the fords of the Jordan, and the city gate was barred behind them.

Then Rahab climbed up to the roof and sat down beside the spies in the dark.

"I know your God has given you this land," she said. "Since we heard how the sea dried up before you, our hearts have melted. There is no courage left in anyone here because of you. Now swear to me that when you come, you will spare my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them."

They swore it. She let them down from her window on a rope, straight down the outside of the wall. "Go to the hills," she told them. "Hide there three days, until the searchers return." The spies told her to tie a scarlet cord in that same window, so that her house would be known and spared.

They hid in the hills three days, then crossed the river and came back to Joshua. "The whole land is ours for the taking," they said. "Everyone there is faint with fear of us."
tales.lesson: The most valuable knowledge is of the other side's heart and morale, and it comes from people on the inside, not from guesswork.
tales.why: Joshua's knowing first came, as 13.3 insists, "from people, people who know the enemy's condition": a local insider and two "Returning agents" who "come back and report" (13.5).
tales.living: Who are the people close to the ground in your work or life whose honest report you are not yet asking for?

tales.title: Sinon and the Wooden Horse
tales.source: Virgil, Aeneid, Book II
tales.tale:
One morning, after ten years of war, the Trojans woke to silence. The Greek camp on the shore was empty, the black ships gone from the beach. All that remained on the plain was an enormous horse built of fir planks, taller than the walls.

The people of Troy poured out of the gates to stare at it. Some wanted to drag it into the city as a trophy. Others wanted to burn it, or cut it open. The priest Laocoön came running down from the citadel. "Are you mad? Do you think any gift of the Greeks is free of treachery? I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts." And he hurled his spear into the horse's belly, where it stuck quivering, and something inside it groaned and echoed.

Just then, a group of shepherds came dragging a young man with his hands tied behind him. He had walked up to them on purpose, they said. He gave his name as Sinon, a Greek.

Sinon stood trembling among the jeering crowd and told his tale with tears. Ulysses had hated him, he said, and when the Greeks needed a human sacrifice to win a fair wind home, Ulysses had made sure the lot fell on him. He had broken his bonds the night before and hidden in a marsh until the fleet sailed. Now he had no country and no friends. Let the Trojans kill him if they liked.

Old King Priam took pity on him and ordered his bonds cut. "Tell us then: why did they build this horse?"

Sinon lifted his freed hands to the heavens. The horse was an offering to Minerva, he said, to make up for a sacrilege. The Greek seer had ordered it built so huge that it could never pass through Troy's gates. For if the Trojans brought it inside, Troy would one day carry the war to Greece itself.

At that moment two great serpents rose from the sea, coiled about Laocoön and his sons, and crushed them. The Trojans took it as the goddess's judgement. They broke a gap in their own walls, and with songs and garlands, they hauled the horse inside.
tales.lesson: A false story is most believable when someone appears to risk everything to tell it. Before acting on what a defector or informant says, ask who sent them and what it costs the sender if you believe it.
tales.why: Sinon is Sunzi's doomed agent in action: the enemy staged "false matters" and sent a man to carry them straight into Troy (13.5), knowing he might well die for it.
tales.living: What story have you believed recently mainly because the person telling it seemed so sincere and so vulnerable?
